speechtext:
The House resumed from Thursday, April 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Richardson for an address to Her Excellency the Governor General in reply to her speech at the opening of the session, and on the amendment of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra):
That this House regrets that Your Excellency's advisors continue to show indifference toward the economic and social well-being of lower and middle-income Canadians and contempt for Canadian democratic institutions by dishonouring commitments to the Canadian people with regard to the implementation of the Canada-U.S. trade deal, by abandoning Canadian farm, fisheries and forest workers, by ignoring the dangerous acceleration of concentration of corporate power, by refusing to act properly and firmly to assure public access to and the safety of the Canadian transportation system, by abdicating responsibility for health care, housing and senior citizens, by failing to protect the rights of minorities across Canada, by deserting the federal role in research, technological and economic development, and by circumventing the authority of the House of Commons with regard to the expenditure of public moneys and by presenting Parliament a program empty of anything save a clear desire to dismantle the Canadian social safety net while imposing an oppressive and inequitable fiscal regime.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity that I have had in the Thirty-Fourth Parliament to address the House of Commons. I want to congratulate you and your colleagues most sincerely on your new responsibilities. You discharged those responsibilities in the past with distinction and I am convinced you will do so in the future as well.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext:
I also am a veteran of sixteen and a half years in the House of Commons and want to welcome the new Members. I know that each of them will find the challenges here to be enormously rewarding. I think they will find that new friendships are built and that their time here is an opportunity for them to make a very important contribution to Canada.
I want as well to take the time to congratulate my critics on the opposition side of the House for their responsibilities. I followed with a great deal of interest the releases that were put out by the two opposition Parties with regard to the assignment of shadow Cabinet responsibilities. After a good deal of adding, Mr. Speaker, I discovered that the opposition Parties had appointed no fewer than 14 critics, co-critics, associate critics and assistant associate critics to monitor the health, the welfare, the state of our seniors and the fitness of our nation. All of us should be impressed by this new-found interest on the part of the Opposition. Most important, what is striking to me is that the Opposition has found a formula for work sharing that if it were to apply across the board in Canada, it could eliminate unemployment overnight, which is something I will commend to my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The past six months have been a period of great change for Canadians. In November this Government, once again, received the support of the Canadian people, winning the first back-to-back majority of any Government since that of Louis St. Laurent in 1953. We won support for our policies, for our leadership and for our plans for the future. As Canadians know, we signed the Free Trade Agreement to give Canadians access to larger markets, to provide more jobs and to increase the number of people capable of paying into our system of social benefits rather than simply drawing upon it.
We made a commitment then as we do now that the Free Trade Agreement will not destroy our Canadian culture, deprive us of our water or damage our social programs. Indeed, exactly the opposite is the case. Just as the Auto Pact has brought new prosperity to Canadians, so will the Free Trade Agreement. That prosperity

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. Beatty
will give us the wealth that is necessary to support Canada's cultural life to enhance our environment and to extend our social programs.
Our network of social programs is an integral part of our identity as Canadians. We are proud of the fact that we have one of the finest health care systems anywhere in the world. We see the excellence of this system as one of the features which distinguishes us from our neighbours to the south.

For example, this year in Canada, we will spend some $50 billion, or $2,000 per Canadian, for accessible health care services of superior quality that meet the needs of our population.

That is a lot of money. Spending by my Department in support of health and welfare is, in fact, the largest single program expenditure which this Government makes. Even that figure is eclipsed by our annual interest payments on the national debt. That is why as we continue to improve our system we must do so in a financially responsible manner. We cannot afford to return to the recession of the 1970s and early 1980s when runaway inflation robbed the pensioners of their life savings, of their dignity and independence, when the level of unemployment was so high that young people looking for jobs were told that their skills were not needed. The sound base that we need to protect our social programs is a strong economic system.
Today, Mr. Speaker, some 31 cents of every tax dollar goes just to pay the interest on the mountain of debt that Ottawa has accumulated over the years. Unless action is taken quickly, that figure will grow and it will grow very rapidly indeed. If Canada is to remain solvent, the interest on the national debt is the first payment that must be made each year before anything else is funded, before pensions, health care, cultural programs, the defence of our nation and before environmental protection.
All of the programs that we think are essential for Government to provide for Canadians must share what is left after the interest has been paid. If the interest payments continue to grow unchecked, they will threaten not only our ability to bring in new programs to meet changing conditions but also our ability to maintain the programs which we have today. We owe it to our children upon whom we are piling this enormous debt burden and
to those who depend upon Government to provide essential services to prevent that crisis from developing.
In Monday's Speech from the Throne the Government promised firm leadership in overcoming the environmental threat to our planet. This is a particularly important initiative from a health point of view.
For example, each 1 per cent decrease in the ozone layer can mean a 4 per cent to 6 per cent increase in certain skin cancers. Dirty water or contaminated food supplies can be responsible for food poisoning, cancers, and other disorders. The health of our nation is intimately linked to the safety of our environment, the air that we breathe and the water that we drink.

This Government's commitment to favour sustainable development, to clean up and protect our major waterways and to eliminate the scourge of acid rain will greatly improve the average Canadian's welfare.

This is only one of our commitments to an improved lifestyle. There are others. As we look for ways in the next four years to make progress in building a country where the health and safety of our citizens is paramount, we will be placing new emphasis on AIDS treatment and prevention, dealing with drug abuse, reducing family violence, implementing a child care program, finding better ways to treat diseases of the elderly, continuing the fight against tobacco and alcohol abuse, and launching a Royal Commission on Reproductive Technologies.
There is not time today to discuss all of these vital initiatives. However, I would like to touch on a few of them, starting with AIDS. Canadian doctors identified the first case in 1982. Since then they have reported 2,500 cases. Half have died already.
It is a terrible, fatal disease that is spreading throughout the world. The World Health Organization has estimated that 450,000 people may already have the disease and, in Africa alone, there may be 10 million people who have been infected by the virus that causes AIDS. In the United States AIDS has already claimed more lives than were lost in the Vietnam war.
It would be wonderful to be able to say that we have AIDS beaten. Unfortunately, we cannot do so. We have no effective cure and we do not expect a vaccine until the end of the centuiy. Hundreds of thousands of lives will be lost before the disease is finally eradicated, but it can be beaten if we commit ourselves to finding a solution.
April 7, 1989

The lives of the people affected by the HIV virus can be lengthened and brightened immeasurably if we act in an intelligent and compassionate manner.
Most important, we know how people get the disease, and that it is very difficult to get if the correct precautions are taken.
In the past few weeks I have had the opportunity to meet with a number of groups fighting the disease and to visit an AIDS hospice, Casey House, in Toronto. I was impressed with how many people have become so involved in helping to deal with the epidemic. I was deeply touched by the courage of both the people who are living with AIDS, and of the people who care for them. They left me with a new sense of hope.
Research and education has lengthened the probable life span of someone diagnosed with AIDS from 24 months to as much as 36 months, and possibly more. There has been a resulting change in philosophy from simply helping someone to die with dignity to improving their quality of life and teaching them how to live with the disease.
While I am very concerned about the spread of AIDS, I am also very worried about the misinformation that spreads along with it. A survey conducted in Ontario found that most people do not want to be exposed to AIDS patients. One in five believes that children with AIDS should not be allowed to attend school.
Some public officials have called for the isolation of people with AIDS, in some cases by removing students from school and in other cases by taking away the jobs of people who have AIDS.
Instead of receiving understanding and respect for their human dignity, people with AIDS are faced with losing their families and friends and having their homes and their jobs taken away from them. It is a cruel and a destructive reaction by a society that considers itself compassionate and civilized.
From a public health perspective it would be difficult to think of a better way to spread the disease than to drive those who are afflicted underground.
I have been in contact with my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), to discuss adopting a policy for federal employees encountering AIDS in the workplace. I hope by setting an example at the federal level we can encourage other Governments and organizations to adopt guidelines which are reason-
The Address-Mr. Beatty
able and safe, and which respect individual rights and human dignity.
We are working hard at the federal level to improve our research and develop our educational programs. We have established a Federal Centre for AIDS and have so far committed $168 million to research, education, and community outreach.
AIDS is a problem that respects no national borders. To stop its spread we will have to pool our resources and information at the international level. For this reason we have dedicated $17.5 million to the World Health Organization's Global Program on AIDS and, in lune, we will host 10,000 participants from around the world to the Fifth International Conference on AIDS in Montreal.
There are a number of other health and welfare issues that also need urgent attention.
As the father of two children, I am keenly aware that there is not a community in Canada where illicit drugs are not available. When I was Solicitor General I was shocked to receive estimates by the RCMP which indicated that each year Canadians spend almost as much on illegal drugs as they do on the defence of our country- over $10 billion dollars a year.
Our police forces have been very good at enforcing our laws and dealing strongly with traffickers, but the more that I learn about the issue, the more I realize that simply enforcing laws will not free this country from illegal drugs. Even in prisons, where we maintain 24 hour supervision, we are not able to get rid of drugs completely-
The difficulty, of course, is that if we dwell exclusively on enforcement, we are focusing attention on the symptom and not on the cause. Enforcement is essential, and we are committed to taking the profit out of crime, but we cannot deal with the issue by force alone. We have to provide treatment, adequate legislation and, most important, we have to remove the demand for drugs.
Last month I signed seven federal-provincial agreements which will provide funding for alcohol and drug abuse programs throughout Canada. I expect to be signing similar agreements with other provinces over the next few weeks. These agreements, which will provide $20 million this and each subsequent year, are part of our Government's five-year National Drug Strategy, designed to help those caught up the in the vicious circle of drug abuse.

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. Beatty
Our current legislation is complex and not totally responsive to emerging trends in drug abuse. The recent increase in the use of "designer drugs" and "look alike drugs" which are not covered by the Narcotic Control Act or the Food and Drug Act is an ongoing problem.
It is a problem which will be addressed shortly when we introduce legislation on psychoactive substance control to control the sale of those new drugs. The Bill will strengthen our ability to combat traffickers, while removing obstacles to the proper medical and scientific use of psychoactive substances.
One of the awful things about drug abuse is that it usually involves our young people. The more I learn about the problem, the more convinced I am that this is only one area where the needs of our youth are not being fully met today.
A truly civilized and caring society must put a priority on our children. Since 1971 the proportion of one-income families has fallen to 25 per cent of all families, while the number of two-income families has risen to almost half. Combined with this is the fact that the number of single parent families is rising rapidly.

There is no doubt that child care is an important matter and that the Government must actively support this service. During the past year, the federal Government spent about $625 million on it, as much as all the provinces together.

We have a $100 million Child Care Initiatives Fund which, among other projects, is funding a conference of 1,200, organized by the Canadian Child Day Care Federation, being held in Winnipeg as we speak. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stated in his address yesterday, we remain committed to implementing a national child care program. Until we pass new legislation, we will continue to support provincial funding of child care programs through the Canada Assistance Plan for those families most in need.
I am also deeply concerned about the incidence of family violence and child abuse in Canada. A 1987 report by the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women estimated that as many as one million women in Canada may be battered each year by the men they live with. The Badgley Report stated that 42 per cent of the
population have been victims of unwanted sexual acts during their lives and that most of the victims have been children. Those are shocking statistics. They require Government action.
Family violence inflicts devastating costs on individuals, on families and on society as a whole. That damage, both physical and emotional, can have long-term effects on people's lives.
We are currently in our first of a four-year program which involves six federal Departments and $40 million to help to address the problem of family violence. One of the cornerstones, Project Haven, is a program operating through CMHC to build 500 new emergency shelter units across Canada. All together our new shelters will enable us to house an additional 25,000 battered women and children each year.
Because we recognize the importance of community participation, we funded 89 projects last year to improve our response to family violence. These projects range from a national survey of elder abuse to sensitivity training for teachers, doctors and lawyers who may be able to detect and help in instances of abuse. The sexual abuse of children is one of the best examples of the painful and concealed problem which must be confronted openly and honestly.
We have many projects and substantial funding devoted to this problem, but realize that there is a pressing need for better information on what is often a family's deepest and darkest secret. For this reason I have a special advisor on child sexual abuse, Mr. Rix Rogers, who will be reporting to me by this fall on how best to proceed with federal initiatives.
[Translation\
Finally, we must deal with an aging society. During the next 15 years, the number of elderly in Canada will more than double. We must find ways to help seniors age serenely, while maintaining their independence and quality of life as long as possible.

It is heart-breaking to see an otherwise healthy senior citizen whose mind has been afflicted by Alzheimer's disease or has been crippled by osteoporosis. The Department of National Health and Welfare will commit an average of $4 million each year to research into diseases which inhibit the independence of our older people. Our challenge is to achieve a healthy and productive life for every Canadian.
April 7, 1989

These are just some of the areas which I believe deserve more attention. Mr. Speaker, you will see a renewed commitment in the fight against AIDS and drug abuse. We will develop further our programs on child sexual abuse and family violence, the hidden tragedies which can destroy people's lives. We will encourage research into diseases associated with aging so that seniors can have lives of independence and dignity.
Today, April 7, is World Health Day. In Canada we are blessed with high standards for health and quality of life which are not shared by much of the rest of the world. In many countries, the issue is not the quality of life, it is survival of the self. As we develop our health system through legislation, research and education, we must help Canadians to help themselves, and also to help those who are less fortunate.

We have reason to be proud, but we must also be realistic about the problems facing us. I have the firm hope that by working together, we can make real improvements.

It is a challenge that is worthy of us all. It is one that will pay very rich rewards indeed if we succeed.

speechtext: Are there questions or comments?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two short comments and questions to ask of the Minister of National Health and Welfare(Mr. Beatty). As he began his remarks he talked about the mountain of debt that the Government has got to work with. I am very concerned about that, as are all Canadians.
I just wondered if he would be more explicit. My understanding, as I go back through the records, is that in 117 years before this Government took over the mountain of debt it had accumulated was somewhere in the $150 billion to $160 billion range. In the next four or five years this Government has apparently run it up to an accumulated deficit of somewhere in the range of $220 billion or $225 billion. I am wondering just how much responsibility for that mess his Government is willing to take.
As well, the Minister spoke about the useless unemployment that was created before his Government took
The Address-Mr. Beatty
over. I am wondering if he would look into or admit to the use of bureaucratic means to achieve less unemployment. I refer to the situation that applies in many rural areas where the unemployment insurance department refuses people unemployment insurance unless they will abandon their small communities and go into the cities for jobs after they have lost jobs in those small communities. Those people no longer show up in the statistics. They are just as unemployed as they were before.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's questions and I will try to deal with them in a serious way. The issue of debt is one which is continuing to grow in Canada. We are proud of the fact that this Government took a deficit of some $38 billion which we inherited and in each of the four years following that we were able to cut that federal deficit and ultimately to reduce it by some $10 billion a year. But that is not good enough.
What we are doing is simply reducing the rate at which the national debt continues to grow. If our concern in this Parliament is to provide for our children in a way that is compassionate, that understands and anticipates their needs, it is important that we not simply defer to future generations the responsibility for coming to grips with that growing national debt.
Most important, as the Minister charged with the responsibility for Canada's social programs, I know that when we reach a stage where 31 cents out of every dollar that is being raised from the taxpayers of Canada is going just to service the interest on the national debt, and that this figure continues to grow year after year, it poses a very real threat to the very survival of Canada's social programs.
The Hon. Member raises a question in which there was a partisan element, but I think the question was a serious one. It deserves a serious response.
Canadians from one coast to another have a right to expect a serious debate in Parliament and across the country about, first, whether we acknowledge as a priority that Canada's economic house has to be put in order, that the Government of Canada is not immune from the laws of economics, that we cannot repeal them and that the same rules govern ordinary households, small businesses or family farms have to apply to Government as well. One cannot constantly be spending more money than one is bringing in without very serious problems indeed.

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. Beatty
Does every Member of Parliament acknowledge that there is a critical and growing problem with this mountain of federal debt? That is the first question.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why didn't you do something about it over the last four years?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Exactly. Let us start with an acknowledgement from all sides of the Elouse-if we can get it-that there is a real problem. Then let us have honest solutions proposed, not sophistry, not sleight of hand, but honest solutions proposed from all sides of the House about how to attack this. What we have seen, Mr. Speaker, in the House of Commons in Question Period and in debate over the course of this week is constant calls by Members of Parliament to increase spending, not to make any cuts in any areas, not to change the tax system but to simply defer to future generations dealing with that national debt.
Second, the hon. gentleman asked me about unemployment. I will respond to it very quickly. I also represent a rural area. What I have seen since 1984 is a dramatic turn around in terms of the opportunities for Canadians to participate fully in the labour force. This has happened across Canada where some 1,300,000 new jobs have been created. This is not sleight of hand. It is real, and I would welcome the Hon. Member to come to my constituency, my rural area. I would be pleased to show him an example of Canadians who have been able to find productive and meaningful work, not work-fair, not hand-outs and short-term jobs provided by Government, but meaningful, constructive, productive, challenging and secure jobs in the private sector as a result of the new economic climate. We are determined to build on that to provide new opportunities for other Canadians as well.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I found the Hon. Minister's remarks on AIDS very sensitive and important. Just a couple of weeks ago I attended a funeral for one of my campaign workers, a person I have known for a long time, who died of this terrible disease. I have read Randy Shilts' book, And the Band Played On, I believe it is called, which demonstrated the American response as pretty pathetic. Health care was held back by discrimination and by bureaucratic inertia. It was sometimes held back by outright lies to the people in that it was known that the blood banks were probably contaminated and nothing was done about that for at least a year. The book is a pretty sad indictment.
I hope that the Hon. Minister's and his Department's actions Are as strong as his words on this matter. He made a reference to setting an example at the federal level. I would draw his attention to the work of the City of Vancouver, especially the Board of Education, and the work that was done there at the municipal level. It has not been the federal level that has been so active there. It has been the municipalities that have dealt with the matters of discrimination. I would compare the response by the elected officials and the politicians of the City of Vancouver, for example, with the pathetic and ignorant response of Andy Haydon from the greater Ottawa regional district, or whatever it is called. So I hope the Minister will look at what Vancouver has done.
What occurred to me in reading the material was that here we have our scientists, the disease control centre, the American scientists, the world scientists if you like, looking at solutions, trying to find a vaccine and trying to find ways of treatment, new drugs. There is a drug called pentamidine, as I understand it, which helps with pneumonia cases. The Canadian Government was very slow to allow people with AIDS to use it. So I want to ask the Minister two questions. One, what is happening in terms of making new experimental drugs available more quickly to people with AIDS? Second, how does he feel about what our scientific efforts should be in research? Should we be doing it here in Canada? Should we be helping the Pasteur Institute in France, or helping the Americans in Atlanta and elsewhere, or should we be doing the research here?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that was a very thoughtful intervention by the Hon. Member. I think any of us who have lost a friend or colleague to AIDS cannot help but be moved by the human element of the disease. Indeed, one of the things that perhaps allows the sort of insensitivity we have seen in all too many cases across Canada is the fact that it is possible to de-personalize it and say this is somebody we do not know who has not touched my life and whose life is in jeopardy, and so I am not threatened by it, that we should ghettoize these people and shut them off from the rest of society.
I could not agree more fully with the Hon. Member that all too often the response has been that when support and assistance were most needed, people with AIDS would be told they could lose their jobs, their family, their housing or their friends as a result of having contracted the disease. It is a disgraceful response by a society which claims to be civilized.
April 7, 1989

Yes, Mr. Speaker, we will look at examples from Vancouver and elsewhere. What disturbs me is that the Hon. Member cited another case where people were not fairly treated, and I fully agree with him. I also read Randy Shilts' book. It is a powerful indictment as to the way in which governments have dealt with the issue of AIDS.
The Hon. Member mentioned one incident that has taken place. There is another involving a school board near Toronto which announced a policy of excluding people with AIDS from the school system. It is disturbing that these are common examples, outrageous examples of what people living with AIDS can in many instances expect from one coast to the other, and that is what we have to change.
The Hon. Member asked me two specific questions. The first is in regard to what is happening as far as making new drugs available. We are working very closely with the drug companies in order to encourage them to bring drugs on to the market. Secondly, we have written to doctors to indicate to them that the Emergency Drug Release Program is in place, that for drugs that are not approved in Canada as yet, emergency release can be made if a doctor gets in touch with the Department of National Health and Welfare and indicates that he or she believes it is important that the drug be released to a patient. This should help to bring these new drugs to patients more quickly.
Mr. Speaker, one of the key issues that has been of concern to people working with AIDS and to the gay community has been the question of drug trials in Canada, the issue of double blind placebo testing. One of the things they have pressed for is to ensure that there are elements as well of so-called open-arm testing which will enable people who are afflicted with the disease to have the opportunity to take advantage of new drugs.
Mr. Speaker, I will be communicating with the drug companies in Canada to make it clear to them that the Federal Government will entertain and approve proposals made by Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers which include responsible programs for open-arm testing. I think this will also help to make these pharmaceuticals more available to people.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member asked me how we should be focusing our limited research dollars. Should we be doing everything in Canada or should we be co-operating internationally? I think the answer must be both. Clearly, AIDS is an issue which cuts across all national borders. It is important that we co-ordinate and not replicate work that is being done elsewhere. There are unique contributions that our researchers here in
The Address-Mr. Mills
Canada can make, and I want to see us identify those in conjunction with people working in the community to target our money where it can be of the greatest benefit to try to find a cure for this dreaded disease.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As a new Member, I consider it a privilege to stand up and address the Speech from the Throne.
Before I become specific on the Speech from the Throne, I would like to go back to an incident that happened in my family about three weeks ago. My 13 year old daughter, Jennifer, came home from school and said, "Dad, we had a career day in class today. We all had to tell the kids what our fathers and mothers were doing in terms of their careers. When I told them you were a Member of Parliament, I received a lot of derision". She said, "I was really embarrassed to tell them. They were not only laughing at me, but they said their parents thought the life of an MP was one where you earn a lot of money but do not do a lot of work, that they see you in the House of Commons every day laughing at one another, making snide remarks at one another". As a result, I kind of reflected and wondered, what am I doing here? How did I get into this?
I went back to 1978 when I first came to this city and met a public servant by the name of Craig Carpenter who had worked for over 25 years in the Public Service of Canada. He was a man who not only loved his job and loved the Public Service, but loved Canada. He provided a lot of inspiration for me.
That experience led to the rare privilege of working with the Rt. Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau. He also loves this country. He understood the Public Service and he knew that the Government of Canada is responsible for policy-making for all Canadians, especially those regions of the countiy that need special help and those people who are disadvantaged.
It was that inspiration that led me to run in Broadview-Greenwood in the last election. When I debated and when I knocked on doors, I would tell my constituents, "If you vote for me, you will not just be voting for someone who will service Broadview-Greenwood. I told them I wanted to go back to Ottawa because I wanted to speak for Canada, not just Broadview- Greenwood, not just Toronto, not just Ontario, but for all of Canada. So with that in mind as my reason for being here, I want to start from the outset with the number one concern in my riding and how it was addressed in the Speech from the Throne, that being free trade.

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. Mills
Over 80 per cent of the people of Broadview-Greenwood voted against the free trade deal. It is not that the people of my riding were against freer trade. I am a business man and I am not against freer trade, but I did say repeatedly that I do not believe that chapter 16 of this contract, unlimited, unregulated investment, will work.
This country was built with regulated investment. I am not against foreign investment. In the last 90 days before Parliament resumed, we saw enough mergers and takeovers. The Government should have been right up front in terms of the free trade deal and should have mentioned right from the outset that it would make sure that the only instrument we have left, the bureau of competition policy, would get all the support it needed to make sure that these mergers and takeovers were in the best interests of Canada. The point I am trying to make is that I just do not understand how we can control the Canadian economy when we have given away the levers.
This is an area in which the Speech from the Throne was sadly lacking. I only hope that over the next little while, the Government will refocus on this issue before we go too far down the track.
The second issue that excited me about the Speech from the Throne, and I say this sincerely, was the issue of the environment.
Before I get any further into my remarks, I want to say that in the last few days when calling home and talking about the Speech from the Throne, many people asked me what a Speech from the Throne is, what it means. I say to those in my constituency and others who are listening today that a Speech from the Throne is like a list you have at home, a list of all the things you are going to do over the next three or four months in your house, whether it be shopping for groceries, making repairs or planning the program you will live by in your house.
I want to tell this House that I think the commitment to the environment in the Speech from the Throne was good. I only hope that the vision in that Throne Speech can become action. If it does not become action, then again we go back to rhetoric. The Minister has an opportunity to be not only a national hero but an international hero if he implements this vision.
Thinking of the environment, I want to touch on Meech Lake for a minute. I ran in my riding promoting the amendments to Meech Lake. Make no mistake about it, it was a serious issue in Broadview-Greenwood. Many people were focusing on the Meech Lake Accord. One of the things we talked about was national programs.
National programs create national will and from national will we get patriotism. I believe that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) has an opportunity to make sure, through the issue of the environment, that we create national will. No province should be allowed to opt out of any national program dealing with the environment. This will lead this Minister of the Environment to realize that just maybe there is room for one or two amendments in the Meech Lake Accord. I think his environment portfolio will lead to that realization.
The environment is not just a national issue, it is an international issue. This Government tends to think of cutting, cutting, cutting. It should focus more on creativity. I want to be constructive here. The Hon. Member who spoke previously spoke about using this House in a positive way. I want to participate in this House in a positive way, so I want to throw some creativity at the Minister of the Environment.
For many years, we have been known for our peacekeeping forces around the world, in Cypress, the Middle East and elsewhere. Why can this Minister not organize environmental forces that will go around the world in times of crisis? The incident in Valdez would have been one place where the Minister could have sent a special environmental force. The environment is not a local or national issue, it is an international issue, and I do not know of a Government in the world that, in a moment of crisis, would turn down a special Canadian force on the environment. I hope the Minister will consider this a constructive idea.
When I was walking along Rideau Street the other night, I passed by the armouries on Wurtemburg Street and saw the millions of dollars worth of equipment sitting there idle. We have to turn some of these forces into constructive use for the environment.
As well, I want to address you, Mr. Speaker, on the issue of the environment. My House of Commons business card is on recycled paper, but I could not get the House of Commons to print this business card because it was not printed on Canadian paper. If we are to be serious about the issue of the environment, we should begin right here in this House. The Speaker should
April 7, 1989

consider a directive that all Members of Parliament use recycled paper for their cards and stationery. If we are to be serious about this, it should start right here in this House.
I want to continue speaking about the environment for a few more minutes. My riding is very excited about hosting this September the first populace summit on the environment in the Don Valley in Toronto, and I must say we are getting terrific support from the Department of the Environment and from the Minister of the Environment, and the diplomatic corps in the community is coming together. This is the kind of action that we need on a constant basis if we are to get ahead of this issue.
Being very specific again, I want the House to know that I share many of the concerns about the deficit, but as everyone has to believe on this side of the House, the deficit should not be put on the backs of those people who are least capable of handling it. Again, we have an opportunity to look at the deficit in a different way. Why not create a larger economic pie? Why not use environmental technology?
In Vancouver, there is an organization that has created clean air technology, Ballard Industries on the North Shore. They need $10 million to go into production, and by the turn of the century, they could have a billion-dol-lar industry which will create tens of thousands of new jobs. The Government would get all kinds of support in creating new environmental technology which will serve not only the environment but our deficit.
There is an organization in Burlington, Ontario, that is working on reverse osmosis. We should get behind these organizations that for years have been suffering without support because the environment was not at the top of the agenda. If we can give them that support right now, I think they will generate the kind of money that will address the deficit in a constructive way.
That is why the Government has to be very careful in the next four years. For the last while, the focus of the Government has been on the bankers it knows and the armaments it builds up. It must shift its emphasis to the mouths we have to feed and the environment we have to protect. That is where we should be going.
The Address-Mr. Mills
I also want to deal with the section in the Speech from the Throne about the caring nation. I could not get over the lack of concern in specific terms for the senior citizens of Canada. The Government, in its very first Budget, shook the seniors of Canada in an unprecedented way. I would have thought it would have been much more sensitive in light of what has been going on, and I think this not just because seniors represent 50 per cent of the riding of Broadview-Greenwood.
The seniors of Canada have worked for years to make this country what it is. I will not prejudge the Budget, because I do not know what is in it, but God forbid that this Government should tamper with the seniors of Canada again. I can only hope that that will not be the case.
I also want to talk about another specific issue. In my riding a basement apartment less than 600 square feet rents for about $1,350 a month. How can a single mother or father handle that?
The Government has talked about a national day care program and its legislation, Bill C-144, was ready to proceed. While it needs amendment, we must begin an action plan on this issue immediately. A national day care program is essential, not only for ridings like Broadview-Greenwood but throughout the country. It is another area where the vision must become a reality.
My last point about a caring society concerns drugs. In my riding drugs are being sold to children in grade school. Some four months ago a principal of a grade school in my riding came to me with a mason jar filled with syringes. He said he had found it under the portable classrooms.
The drug issue is very serious and I suggest the Government consider establishing a drug czar who would have access to all the communications resources, technical resources and the resources of the RCMP. The problem is already far out of hand and God forbid that we should see an environment developing here similar to the one in Washington today. We should learn from the example in Washington and prevent the problem from occurring here. The Government should start by appointing a drug czar who would bring special focus to this problem.
I have talked about free trade, the environment, seniors, day care and drugs. Now let me make a point about the Public Service of Canada. I have noticed in the last six months that there is a great deal of lethargy in the Public Service of Canada at present. The Government

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. Mills
should be addressing this problem. Many do not realize that the Public Service of Canada is the engineroom for this Chamber. I have talked to many public servants who believe in their jobs as a vocation. Many public servants believe in Canada but they have faced too much pressure as a result of cuts imposed by the Government, cuts that have not always been correct. I make this statement constructively.
I am not proposing to fatten the Public Service, but many good public servants have been ruined because the Government has made cuts in the wrong area. For example, our immigration officers here and abroad are under tremendous pressure. Many other public servants in other departments should be given the proper assistance to implement the policies that come from this Chamber. It has been said that you are only as good as the factory. The factory must be in good shape but right now the Public Service is demoralized and needs serious attention.
Finally, I want to talk about multiculturalism. I am not convinced that the present approach to multiculturalism is the correct one. We should take an entirely different approach to the area of multiculturalism.
The Government should consider a super ministry of culture which makes multiculturalism our national symbol. This issue has been given simple add-on status to a department for too long. I know that my co-critic shares this view.
I hope this matter is put on the agenda early in the Government's mandate. Perhaps we can learn from Walt Disney who had inscribed on his hard hat, when he was building Disneyland, the word "imagineering". It is a blend of imagination and engineering which made Disneyland what it is. We have to apply that blend of imagination and engineering to much of the public policy we discuss in this House.
In conclusion, it was 10 years ago when Craig Carpenter and Pierre Elliott Trudeau inspired me to get into public life. I only hope that our activities in this House in the next few years will cause me and all of us to set an example that will encourage other Canadians to get into public life. My ultimate satisfaction will be for my
daughter Jennifer to finally go back to school and be proud that her father is an MP.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows what the Party position is. We in this House voted for and supported the Meech Lake Accord, with nine amendments which the press has never reported. I realize that the Hon. Member's Party has amendments as well, but not as many.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not as good.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the new Member of Parliament for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Mills) for sharing with the House and all colleagues a fresh vision from Broadview-Greenwood. It behooves that Member in the far corner to ask a question about the position of this Party on Meech Lake as opposed to taking a look at his own Party.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is an opportunity for the Government and the private sector to get together. I salute the Loblaw Company, the largest food company in the world, which has decided to get behind our world summit on the environment in the Don Valley. We now have the support of all levels of government, the Province of Quebec, the Province of Ontario. We will have over 70 speakers coming from around the world. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It being eleven o'clock, the House will now proceed to Statements by Members, pursuant to Standing Order 30.
April 7, 1989

subsubtopic: MIDDLE EAST-CONTACTS BETWEEN CANADA AND PALESTINIAN LIBERATION ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recent initiative by the Government of Canada to upgrade its level of contact with the Palestinian Liberation Organization and to reinforce its support for self-determination for the Palestinians is to be commended.
Canada has long been well regarded by all parties in the Middle East as a peacekeeper and a moderate, trusted voice. This move will further reinforce that position.

maintopic: WITHDRAWAL FROM SALE OF DRUG ADVOCATED
WITHDRAWAL FROM SALE OF DRUG ADVOCATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada is the only country in the world still selling Diclectin, the generic copy of Bendectin, an anti-nausea drug which has been linked to birth defects when taken by pregnant women.
Bendectin was voluntarily withdrawn by its manufacturer in 1983 because of the high number of lawsuits brought by parents on behalf of children with birth defects linked to this drug. Why Canada would continue to allow the generic copy to be sold when so much uncertainty surrounds this product is incomprehensible.
The Government claims the drug has not been withdrawn because there is insufficient proof it causes birth defects. Many Canadian families do not agree. These people have not a shadow of a doubt that their child's defects are directly related to this drug.
I therefore call on the Government to launch a full investigation immediately into the drug Bendectin and its generic Diclectin, and to prohibit the company from marketing this drug until such time as it is proven safe for use.
I think Canadian families have every right to be heard in this matter rather than just a word given to the Department of Health and Welfare and by the manufacturer of this drug. The Department of Health and Welfare has never done an investigation into this drug.
TRIBUTE TO DYNAMISM OF SEPT-iLES

Mr. Speaker, the Chamber of Commerce of Sept-iles is celebrating its 35th anniversary this year. The Chamber is organizing several events, including an evening to recognize its former presidents. This will be held on Saturday, April 8 and will highlight the involvement of many women and men in improving the community, economic and cultural life of Sept-iles.
I am pleased to call on all Members of the House of Commons to join me in paying special tribute to all the people of Sept-iles who over the last 35 years have worked together to make their community a dynamic, well-organized city. Special mention goes to Gustave Blouin, one of the founders of the Chamber who represented the riding of Manicouagan in the House of Commons for many years.

Mr. Speaker, two days ago it was reported that the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) was considering cutting, slashing and/or privatizing all or part of the National Arts Centre. Such a move would be viewed with dismay by the vast majority of Canadians, Canadians who view the promotion of arts and culture as a national priority and one for which the National Arts Centre is a leading institution.
Moreover, slashing the National Arts Centre would be devastating to my riding of Nepean and the National Capital Region as a whole. Were the NAC Orchestra to be privatized, a move that is under consideration, the resulting hunt for corporate funding would have a chilling effect on the fund-raising ability of all the region's cultural groups.
Instead of another "Night at the Opera", and in keeping with the "commitment to the growth and development of Canada's cultural life" outlined in the Throne Speech, I urge the Minister of Communications to look for ways of increasing funding for arts and culture in Canada rather than ways of cutting it back.

April 7, 1989

Mr. Speaker, the Fire Services Exemplary Medal was established in 1985 and is one of three national medals honouring Canadians who serve the public in dangerous professions. Medals were previously established for the police in 1983 and Correctional Service employees in 1984.
Firefighters who have served 20 or more years with exemplary service are eligible to receive this honour only if they were active in service on or after August 29,1985. Many Canadians who risked their lives in this honourable and dangerous profession are being discriminated against because they retired on or before August 28, 1985.
I urge the federal Government to recognize the great, personal risk taken by these Canadians, and to honour all who qualified on or before August 29, 1985.

subtopic: LEBANON-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE CEASEFIRE AND GREATER ACCESS TO CANADIAN CONSULAR SERVICES
LEBANON-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE CEASEFIRE AND GREATER ACCESS TO CANADIAN CONSULAR SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, an immense world tragedy is now taking place before our eyes in Lebanon. What is happening there is unacceptable and the Government of Canada must be very active in the United Nations and initiate joint action with other countries for an immediate cease-fire.
More than 200,000 wonderful Lebanese Canadians of all religions beg us to increase our efforts to help poor, beloved Lebanon. We must support Lebanon's sovereignty and independence. Like the countries of the European Economic Community, the Vatican, France and the United States, all allies and friends of Canada, we must insist on the unconditional withdrawal of all non-Lebanese armed forces, except for the UN peacekeeping force. And we must offer diplomatic assistance to Lebanon in this cruel phase of its history.
I urge the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to please open a temporary office in Cyprus for all the consular and diplomatic requirements of Lebanon, since it is absolutely unacceptable and unthinkable to ask the Lebanese to go to Damascus for their consular needs. So I ask the Minister, the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs, to whom I
will not put any questions today as I had warned him, to take this action. And I think that the 200,000 Lebanese Canadians of all religions will be eternally grateful to him.
* *

Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty) stated this morning, April 7 is World Health Day. The international community has set this day aside to encourage us to reflect on health as a precious individual asset and to recognize the right of all people to health. It is also a day to remind us that health is the responsibility of both the individual and the community.
While action by Governments at all levels is an essential element in improving the health of people, it is not the whole answer. Individuals must share the responsibility for their own health by adopting healthy lifestyles. The acceptance of such personal responsibility depends greatly on the ability of our health workers, educators, and decision-makers to communicate appropriate health information to every man, woman, and child. In an effort to address that need, the theme of this year's World Health Day is "Let's talk health/Parlons sante".

Mr. Speaker, in the last Parliament, I introduced a Private Member's Bill and a motion to give Canadians who work abroad, for example, the workers for CUSO, and other non-government organizations, the right to vote in Canadian general elections. Canadian diplomats and soldiers can vote but not others who are working abroad. I had a good hearing in committee, but when the legislation came forward there was no change.
About a week ago I saw the Soviet elections. Every Soviet citizen working or vacationing in Canada went to the Soviet embassy and voted on election day. I say, Mr. Speaker, are the Soviets more democratic than we Canadians? I ask you, Mr. Speaker, let's have a little more perestroika here in Canada. Let's catch up to the new Soviet democracy and allow our non-government organization workers who work abroad to vote in Canadian elections by going to a Canadian embassy.
April 7, 1989

subtopic: PRIORITY SOUGHT FOR USE OF CANADIAN WINES AT PARLIAMENTARY FUNCTIONS
PRIORITY SOUGHT FOR USE OF CANADIAN WINES AT PARLIAMENTARY FUNCTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, within the past few weeks the federal Government and the Government of Ontario reached a final agreement to ensure compensation is given to Ontario grape growers for the removal of surplus vines as well as of those vines which do not yield the varieties of grapes conducive to producing premium wines. This action will allow the grape and wine industry to further develop high quality wines.
Given the extreme competitiveness of today's market, the continued enhancement of premium wines is crucial to the long-term survival of the Canadian wine industry.
It is very important that all Canadians realize that we have in our own backyard, wines which have won awards at many international competitions.
In support of this industry, we as parliamentarians should continue to ensure that Canadian wines are given priority when planning events to be held in conjunction with the House of Commons, as well as events sponsored by the various political Parties and associations.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in recognition of World Health Day. While this is a very important occasion around the globe, I would like to draw Hon. Members' attention to a health crisis which exists right here in our own country.
It is no secret that the health of Canada's aboriginal peoples is a most pressing issue. Housing shortages have led many to live in sub-standard housing. Inadequate water and sewer infrastructures have contributed to the poor health of First Nations. Insufficient funding for health care services and facilities does not meet the increasing needs of those trying to rectify the situation.
In recent months we have heard of PCB contamination, mercury pollution, and tuberculosis outbreaks in some native communities, some of which are located in my riding.
I urge the Government to make a firm commitment to improved funding for programs which will ensure that the health of our First Nations people is restored.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted with the strong emphasis on the environment in the Throne Speech.
As a Member of Parliament who is concerned about our quality of life and has been militant in environmental affairs in the last few years, I wholeheartedly support the various initiatives announced in the Throne Speech: to promote sustainable development; to enlarge the responsibilities of the Department of the Environment to ensure that environmental issues are fully considered in the course of its decision making; to negotiate an acid rain accord with the United States; to develop and adopt clean production processes; to improve the quality of our water; and to establish the Environmental Partners Fund.
These initiatives are a response to my own expectations and demands and those of my fellow citizens.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the Progressive Conservative Government has made the environment one of its top priorities and intends to continue the unique leadership it has shown in this area.

subtopic: PROGRESS TOWARD INTERNATIONAL TEST BAN TREATY
PROGRESS TOWARD INTERNATIONAL TEST BAN TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 5 an unprecedented breakthrough was announced in the effort to end nuclear test explosions. Under the terms of the partial test ban treaty signed in 1963 by Khruschev and Kennedy, a conference must be convened to discuss its conversion into a comprehensive test ban if so requested by one-third of the 116 countries which originally ratified it.

April 7, 1989
The breakthrough came last week, Mr. Speaker, when Tanzania added its name to a list of 38 countries calling for the amendment conference. It is incomprehensible that the Canadian Government remains opposed to this progressive move which would open the doors to further dialogue on the reduction of nuclear arms. To doom negotiations to failure before they have begun is very unwise.
We must do all we can to rid the world of life-threatening nuclear arms now, and our Government should encourage and support the amendment conference which would bring us closer to this goal.

subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL SALES TAX-FORECAST OF IMPACT
PROPOSED NATIONAL SALES TAX-FORECAST OF IMPACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today Liberal and Tory Finance Ministers from across the country are gathering behind closed doors cutting a deal on a national sales tax. That deal will be one of the biggest tax grabs in the history of our country.
How big is that Tory tax grab going to be? The former Chairman of the Finance Committee said some $10 billion. The Ontario Minister of Finance says $14 billion. I suggest that ordinary Canadians hang onto their wallets because this tax will amount to about $1,000 for every man, woman, and child.
That Tory tax grab will mean a sales tax in many provinces of 16 per cent, 17 per cent, 18 per cent, and 19 per cent. For the ordinary Canadian people this will be recessionary. It will drive up the inflation rate, interest rates, and unemployment.
I say to the Canadian people it is time to stand up and say no to the Tory tax grab. Say no to the Tories trying to take more money from your pockets. No.

subtopic: DEMAND THAT OFFICIALS APOLOGIZE TO COMMUNITY ORGANIZATION
DEMAND THAT OFFICIALS APOLOGIZE TO COMMUNITY ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several weeks ago the immigration office in Toronto refused to provide a briefing on the new refugee legislation to a
community organization in the community of Jane Finch in my riding of York West. The reason for this was that the officers said the community was "too dangerous" to enter.
I wish to tell the Minister and the Government that this was a slap and a severe blow to the integrity and the fibre of that proud community.
Jane Finch is not some simple geographic intersection. It is a proud community made up of proud, hard working Canadians, which deserves full and equal service. In addition to slamming the integrity of the community the Government is also undermining the principle of equal service to all Canadians, regardless of who they are and where they live.
I call upon the Minister of Immigration (Mrs. Mac-Dougall) to reverse this very offensive behaviour by her officials, and to render a public apology to the community and immediately establish a proper briefing for an organization that is willing to co-operate and work hand-in-hand with the Government on refugee legislation.
The community is sick and tired of people who cast innuendoes and veiy easy stigmas on a community that has to work very, very hard to refute unfair allegations.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay tribute to Murdo Martin who served as the Member of Parliament for Timmins from 1957 to 1968, and who passed away in January.
Murdo's years of service to our country started during the Second World War when he served overseas with the Canadian Army.
Murdo was a firefighter and was very active in his union where he became the president. He also was president of the Cochrane District Labour Council and of his local credit union.
He presented himself as the CCF candidate in Timmins in the 1957 general election, an election which he won. He stood for better things for working people. He survived the Diefenbaker sweep of 1958 and helped the CCF transform itself into the NDP in 1961. He also won re-election in 1962, 1963, and in 1965.
April 7, 1989

I believe that the greatest tribute to Murdo's political skill and commitment to his constituents was this string of re-elections.
Since leaving this Chamber, Murdo remained active in the local NDP and labour movement in Timmins. His help and advice to me will always be remembered, and his commitment to working people will never be forgotten.
May I conclude by offering my sympathies to Grace Martin and the rest of his family. Timmins and this Chamber have lost a great friend.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: FEDERAL SUBSIDIES FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Yesterday the Canadian Human Rights Commissioner tabled his annual report. Among the other things he had to say was this:
An Indian youngster in Canada has a better chance of being sent
to prison than completing university.
The Human Rights Commissioner singled out the Minister of Indian Affairs for criticism for his decision to limit federal subsidies for post-secondary education for the native people.
How can the Prime Minister allow his Government to carry on with that disgraceful decision? Does he not understand that for our native people education is the only way out?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FEDERAL SUBSIDIES FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Right Hon. Member for his question. I want to tell him right away that we do agree that education is the way out. That is why we have reviewed the guidelines in order to make them more workable so that more native students can achieve a university degree.
I would like to point out to the right hon. gentleman that since 1984 the budget with respect to post-secondary education for native students has nearly doubled.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL SUBSIDIES FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reply of the Minister ought to be read in conjunction with the Prime Minister's comment some time ago when Bill C-31 was before the House, that post-secondary education would not be cut nor would other facilities to
Oral Questions
our native people as a result of widening the definition of status.

subtopic: RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF FUNDING FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF FUNDING FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
Since the Minister himself answered my question, I have to say he failed to show any sensivity to the Commissioner's comments, and I would therefore repeat what the Chief Commissioner said: An Indian youngster has a better chance of being sent to prison than completing university.
This is a national tragedy.
And the only answer the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development gave the striking students was: Go back to school.
I want to ask the Prime Minister once more to tell his Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to reverse his decision and restore funding for post-secondary education for our Native people.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF FUNDING FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that being the kind of man he is, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition would not want to mislead Canadians by being less than accurate in his rendering of my answers.
First of all, I gave more than one answer. I believe I made it quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that since this program started operating with a budget, it has expanded by 10 per cent. I also said that the program will probably continue to expand as needs increase, and that we are of course considering new needs in terms of Bill C-31 which our Government introduced in order to correct a form of discrimination that has existed in Canada for a long time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I do not think that the House should be any more impressed with that answer than the Commissioner of Human Rights was when he singled the Minister out for criticism in his report.
As the Minister knows, a group of college students are now in their 17th day of a hunger strike to protest a policy which the Commissioner of Human Rights has termed a national tragedy. He has called it a national disgrace. Yet the Minister refuses to meet these students. By his attitude, I want to suggest to him he is

April 7, 1989
Oral Questions
perhaps compounding the potential tragedy that we have here.
Will the Minister, and through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Prime Minister, will the Prime Minister order his Minister to demonstrate some common decency and meet with the students to see whether he cannot recognize that the policy that he is leading is highly discriminatory to a very vulnerable people to whom we owe more than we are giving?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to try to play cuteness with the Right Hon. Member, but I am not impressed with his question either.
On the other hand, I do want to indicate to the House, to all Canadians, and particularly to the people who are directly concerned, that I am taking this issue very seriously, that I am prepared to sit down and discuss with whomever is interested the policy-
With the students?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
I have already indicated that, if it is demonstrated that the policy can be improved, I will look at it, and will obviously be interested in improving the policy.
However, this has to be done in normal circumstances. As I did earlier this week, I again urge the students to put an end to their strike and I will meet with them.
I would like to point out a suggestion that was sent by Lakehead University and Confederation College. They are specifically urging the students to put an end to the strike, and to start a bilateral process, and I am prepared to do that.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs. I have met in private with the Minister, and I have pleaded with him. I have expressed the concerns of those students to the Minister, and I plead again to the Minister to meet with these students.
Does the Minister want to have these students continue their fast over the weekend and have the blood of those students on his hands on Monday morning?
Oh, oh!
I find his comments to be insensitive and irrelevant to the situation at hand. Will the Minister meet with those students?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I will meet with the students as soon as they put an end to their hunger strike, at whatever time they decide.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is the following.
The cap on the education funding restricts the number of native students who want to attend post-secondary education. On that note, I have spoken to the Grand Chief of the Assembly of First Nations, Mr. George Erasmus.
Will the Minister commit to establishing a bilateral consultative process between the federal Government and First Nations native communities, which the Prime Minister committed to in a statement in the House on April, 1985, and put a moratorium on the new policy changes until this consultation process is firmly established and implemented?
The Prime Minister's words were: "There will be no cut to Indian programs". In that statement there was also a statement that inferred that inflation costs would be kept in line with the needs of the native students.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are many questions in that supplementary question. I will try to address all of them, if time is given to me.
First of all I wish to indicate to the House, to all Canadians, and particularly those people interested, that there is already a bilateral process between Grand Chief Erasmus and myself. We have already met.
There is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
We are scheduled to meet Monday on concerns that the Grand Chief may have. Education is one of them. I have been given the report that they have prepared, and we are looking into it. If Grand Chief Erasmus wants to speak to me on post-secondary education specifically on Monday, obviously I will do that. I am open to speak with every Grand Chief in the country on whatever subject they wish, Mr. Speaker, under normal circumstances.
April 7, 1989

With respect to commitments of the Prime Minister and this Government, not only was this program not cut, it has increased 10 per cent in the last two years.
Over 3 years.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: I usually listen to questions. Perhaps I could be given the same courtesy and the Hon. Member would listen to my answers.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Since 1984 expenditures with respect to natives have gone from $2.7 billion to $3.4 billion.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a question on the same serious matter. Today a band of courageous native students entered the 17th day of a hunger strike against the cruel educational policies of the Government.
The Minister has agreed to meet the students, only if they first end their hunger strike. In a spirit of compromise the students have agreed to suspend their strike in order to bring their case to the Minister.
Will the Minister agree now, in response to that compromise, to an immediate meeting with the hunger strikers in order to resolve this crisis and prevent permanent injury to those native students?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
I agree with the suggestion that was made by Lakehead University and Confederation College which states:
In order to resolve the current impasse and, in the true spirit of

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT THE PRIME MINISTER WITHDRAW CERTAIN REMARKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister.
Yesterday during his speech in the House, the Prime Minister got carried away by his own rhetoric and went so far as to say that the Constitution of this country was not worth the paper it was written on.
Today I want to ask the Prime Minister who, as the first legislator of Canada, is responsible for protecting the basic law of this country, whether he will take this opportunity to apologize and withdraw what he said, because he who discredits the Constitution discredits Canada.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT THE PRIME MINISTER WITHDRAW CERTAIN REMARKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1982 the federal Government surrendered the notwithstanding clause to the provinces, thus enabling the provincial legislatures to override decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada, as the Hon. Member well knows, and to ignore the most fundamental rights and freedoms of our society.
Thanks to this clause,-and I am perhaps by these words leaving myself open to further comment by the Hon. Member-the legislatures can pass legislation restricting freedom of conscience, peaceful assembly, association and religion, freedom of thought, opinion and expression, including the freedom of the press.
Therefore, by invoking the clause I condemned yesterday, the legislatures can deny citizens the right to life, liberty and personal security, the right not to be arbitrarily detained or imprisoned, the right to be informed promptly of the reasons of one's arrest or detention, and even worse, of the right to be assisted by counsel, the right to habeas corpus, the right to be presumed innocent until proven guilty, and so forth.
These are some of the rights that may be suppressed by a given legislature, and this quite extraordinary clause was agreed to in the 1981-82 negotiations by the federal Government.
It always has been my contention that a constitution should unite a nation. The Hon. Member for Shefford knows perfectly well that the Quebec National Assembly vigourously rejected the proposal made in 1981-82. First and foremost, however, the Constitution must protect
the most fundamental rights of a country's citizens. And as you see, that is not the case.
That is why I believe the Constitution drafted in 1981-82 leaves much to be desired.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the Prime Minister. If he was so appalled at the provisions in the "notwithstanding clause", how come at Meech Lake he forgot to have that provision removed?
After the partisan debating he had yesterday, does he not feel he is moving the "notwithstanding clause" into a symbol for Quebec, pushing Quebec's Premier into making statements he never made before, opening a "from now on" era and becoming a symbol of the "Quebec" way of doing things? Does the Prime Minister feel he advanced the debate yesterday, or does he not rather feel he may have undermined an eventual withdrawal of the "notwithstanding" clause, but most of all his Meech Lake Agreement?

Mr. Speaker, I had no idea I was going to wound the feelings of the Hon. Member who himself does not beat around the bush when referring to Government proposals. He never had any qualms about speaking his mind. . .
Not on the Constitution!

Not on the Constitution! Oh no! Not on the Constitution! But the former Prime Minister gave his views on the Constitution as reported in Robert Sheppard and Michael Valpy's book, and I quote:

When Mr. Trudeau was asked if he considered the 1981
Constitution a success he replied, "No, I consider it an abject
failure".
In my view, the basic constitutional document should do two things; first of all, unify the country. To me, a constitution that is not supported across the land, in this case Quebec, is not a true constitution in the first place. Secondly, a constitution should protect the basic rights of citizens. But in this Constitution the legislator has been allowed to infringe upon basic rights. Certainly the Hon. Member will agree the aim of Meech Lake was not to fill offhand all the gaps, but rather to bring them... Careful! And as the Hon. Member will tell his colleagues, it was to finally get Quebec back into the constitutional fold, after having been left out.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: The purpose of this Bill is to change the definition of Section 173 of the Criminal Code. The "peeping Tom" provision of the Criminal Code only permits charges under that provision to be laid for an offence occurring at night. Someone who prowls on the property of another in the daytime cannot be charged under the "peeping Tom" provision of the Criminal Code. The amendment would remove the words "at night", permitting such charges to be laid at any time. This is an important amendment and has the support of several women's organizations in Canada.
