speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The period for questions and comments is now terminated. Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Kamloops (Mr. Riis).

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure and an honour to participate in the debate. I want to thank Members opposite for the arrangements that were made to make this possible today.
I want to begin my presentation in the House today by saying that I believe November 21, 1988-the day of the federal election-will go down in Canadian history as likely the second most significant date. The first, of course, being July 1, 1867, when we saw the beginning of Canada formally occur. Then 121 years later, on November 21, 1988, with the re-election of the Conservative Government we saw the beginning of the end of Canada as we have known it.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Really?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The reason is that the Government decided to proceed with the Free Trade Agreement with the United States, which is the dismantling of Canada, the reorganizing of Canada, the rearranging of Canada to make us an integral part of the United States. What has to be recognized is that the Government lacked the support of the people of Canada generally.
When you look at the way people voted, not how the constituencies or gerrymandering and so on occurred to take advantage of the political situation, and their voting patterns, you will find that 57 per cent of the people voted againsts the Conservatives in the last general election. People in eight our of ten provinces voted against the Conservatives and people in two out of two Territories voted against the Conservatives.
We are talking about a minority position, and yet the Government has taken that minority position because of the way the country is organized around constituencies and decided to end Canada as we know it and integrate us into the United States. This was due in large part not because the people of Canada understood clearly the implications of the trade deal, but because through an incredible amount of election advertising, the likes of which we have never seen before, Canadians were sold a bill of goods, and to a certain extent, were misrepresented and misled. Look at the advertising that went into the free trade deal. The Progressive Conservative Party of Canada alone spent over $5 million. The large corporate sector, including the Business Council on National Issues, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, groups like
April 7, 1989

the Fraser Institute and the major media outlets, spent in combination $19 million.
The lowest blow of all is that this deal had not been sanctioned by the Parliament of Canada, yet the Government felt it had the go-ahead to spend taxpayers' money on an initiative which had not been sanctioned, and paid $32 million for an advertising total of $56 million for the trade deal. Up against that were the individuals from the opposition Parties speaking against the trade deal. The people of Canada were misled through some very misleading advertising, and the Conservatives managed to get 43 per cent of the people's support and that enabled the Government to proceed. That is why I say that November 21, 1988, will be a very historic day in Canadian history. That was the day the end really began.
I do not want to speak today about the trade deal. That is not the purpose of this. The trade deal which the Government signed will haunt this country, this Parliament and this Government forever. We saw immediately after the deal was signed the various companies collapsing and hundreds and thousands of jobs being lost.
I have before me a document that goes on and on: "Gillette in Montreal, 590 jobs; Pittsburgh Paints in Toronto, 139 jobs; Northern Telecom in Belleville, 87ebec, 100 jobs; Chrysler Canada in Ajax, 430 jobs; Taurus Shoes in Quebec, 100 jobs". I could go on for pages and pages listing businesses that have closed down because they have decided to move their operations to the United States or to northern Mexico.
We must recognize that the Government has decided to run the country in a rather unique manner. The House has not sat in the last six months, with the exception of two weeks in December when the Government jammed the trade deal through. It costs $1 million per day when the House does not sit, and we have not sat for six months, with the exception of two weeks.
While the House has not been sitting and while Parliament has not been able to function, what has happened across the country? We have seen interest rates sky-rocket once again. Now they are in the 13 per cent area. Yesterday they inched up again. How high will they go before the Government decides to take action? Will it be 14 per cent, 16 per cent, 18 per cent, or 20 per cent? For a while under a Liberal Government they went
The Address-Mr. Riis
up as high as 22 per cent. How high do interest rates have to go before the Government says that enough is enough?
The Government has recognized that there are two Canadas. There is the Canada of Toronto, and there is the rest of the country. In terms of policy these interest rates reflect a reality in one city of this country, while the rest of the country must pay the price. As a westerner one would be hard pressed to find a single person who would say that this monetary policy is the correct one.
The Premier of Alberta, the Premier of Saskatchewan, the Premier of Manitoba, as a matter of fact, every single Premier came to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and begged him to come to his senses, to stop the interest rate nonsense, and to start bringing down the rates.
I would hope sometime in the debate to hear Members stand up and say that they are in favour of this high interest rate policy; I have not yet heard anyone from the government side or the opposition side say so. Why do we have Members of the House who tolerate this policy which is strangling and smothering the regions in their efforts to dig out of the recessionary times of 1981.
We have seen corporate concentration take place and accelerate, and the focussing of economic, political, and social power into fewer and fewer hands. Since the Government has taken office, which is not too many years-too many but not that many-there have been more than 3,000 foreign takeovers in this country. That means there are 3,000 Canadian companies which are no longer Canadian. No longer are they making decisions about their future in Canada. Those decisions are being made primarily in the United States, Germany, Japan, Hong Kong, or wherever. As we sit here in this session, on average, four foreign takeovers a day are occurring in our country.
As part of that process, corporate concentration and the concentration of power are increasing. Today it is unbelievable, but we are the only western industrialized nation with seven families now controlling 50 per cent of the value of the Toronto Stock Exchange top 300. That type of concentration would not be found in a single other western industrialized nation. What we are doing about it? The Government has instituted policies to

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. Riis
accelerate the process of more and more concentration. That is another one that we have been waiting for.
American Express has come into Canada. It said that it wanted to be a bank in Canada. It is not a bank in the United States or anywhere in the world, but it wanted to have banking status in Canada. The Minister of Finance said that that was fine, and gave that status to American Express. It is not going home without taking the rest of us with them. That is exactly the result.
Do Canadians realize that, because of the amount of foreign ownership and foreign control of our economy, every hour of the day, every hour of the week, every hour of the month, and every hour of the year, $1.5 million leaves our country in the form of dividend payments or payments back to parent companies? That is $1.5 million every single hour of the year because so much of our economy is owned and controlled from outside Canada. Not only is the Government not doing anything to slow or reverse this process, but its policies are accelerating and increasing this situation.
Today we heard the terrible news that the regional disparities in our country are widening, that the gap between rich and poor is widening. A central core around the City of Toronto is prospering and increasing, and the rest of the country is falling relatively further and further behind. This is despicable.
How is the Government reacting to regional disparities increasing in the country, and the increasing gap between the "haves" and the "have nots"? Its response is to cut further support to the regions of this country. That is what the Government is doing in relation to ERDA. In those agreements federal and provision Governments work together to provide assistance and encouragement to develop the regional economies of the country. The Government states that it is not going to do that in the future. It is going to cut back support for the regions of the country. As the Minister from Toronto said during the election "if in the future you want a job, you better move to Toronto". If one lives in Chicoutimi, Comer Brook, Red Deer, Moose Jaw, or Kamloops this Government's idea of your future is to suggest moving to Toronto. That is the type of regional economic expansion programs the Government has in mind.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They won't be able to live there.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
As my hon. friend has indicated, Mr. Speaker, once you get there if you have $300,000 you might be able to purchase a home, if it is available.
We are seeing a Government emerge with a view that its role is to provide encouragement and support for the privileged, the wealthy, the haves. The others, the average Canadian citizen, is on his or her own. It is called the laissez-faire approach. It is the market-place approach.
This country was not built on the free market. From day one the Government of Canada and the provincial Governments have recognized that unless we take action, and to a certain extent are involved in the market, we will have a North American market that will essentially be owned and controlled from the United States. Therefore, we built a national rail system, a national air system, a national highway system, a municipal infrastructure, and a public broadcasting system.
Over the years we took all types of measures to link up and bind the country together with an east-west emphasis. Now the Government has abandoned that thought. This is neo-conservatism at its worst. It is something that would make John Diefenbaker and John A. Macdonald turn in their graves. The Government has decided to abandon what we have struggled with for 122 years in terms of fighting to bind this countiy together into something meaningful. As of the election of November 21, 1988 the Government abandoned that and decided that it was quite prepared to become an extension of the United States.
The Government did not have the mandate to that in 1988. I am confident that in 1992, when the people of Canada finally realize what the Government has done to them, it will be terminated from doing this any further into the future.
I remember when the Hon.Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) was running for the Conservatives. He stated that Government members could not tell the people of Canada what they were going to do "because if we did, they would never vote for us". How right he was. There are times when the Minister for International Trade speaks the truth. He spoke the truth when he said: "If we told the people of Canada what we will do, they would never vote for us".
Does anybody remember during the 1984 election the Government indicating that it wanted to introduce the free trade deal? It was not mentioned even a single time in that campaign. During the campaign of 1988 did anyone from the government benches mention that the
April 7, 1989

Government was going to slash social programs, cut back support for small business, abandon the family farm, and cut back on a whole range of social programs? No. The Government made all kinds of promises.
I have to give the Minister of Finance credit where credit is due. He has now said: "You know all those promises that we made during the election? Well, I am afraid we are going not going to be able to keep them". At least he has been honest and up front. The other day the Minister responsible for regional economic development also was up front when he stated that all those programs to assist the regions in developing their economies would also have to be cut back. The Government says that we have a deficit problem. We have a deficit problem. We have many problems. We have environmental problems. We have deficit and other problems.
When a deficit problem is solved there are two fundamental choices to make. Taxes can be raised on everybody, there can be cut-backs on programs that affect everybody, or something can be done on a specialized basis. This is where the political Parties differ. The Conservative idea of reducing the deficit is to give tax breaks and grants out to the large corporate sector, not to mention the rich and the privileged, with the assumption that they somehow will let this money filter down to assist the economy, and raise everybody's taxes.
As a sensible person, Mr. Speaker, you would say surely to goodness the conservatives would not have that approach. They have that approach. Today, as we sit here in the house of commons, the Ministers of Finance from across the country are meeting with the federal Minister of Finance to find ways and means to implement the new national sales tax.
Do you realize, Mr. sPeaker, what that means to the average Canadian family? To think that on top of the provincial sales tax of 5 per cent, 7 per cent, 9 per cent, the federal Government is now going to pile on its tax. This will mean that when one buys baby diapers or a book, when one goes to the movies or gets drycleaning and laundry done, or when one buys a car, a house or a suit, one will pay 19 per cent or 20 per cent sales tax.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)

speechtext:
He is absolutely false when he says that. There is no sales tax on movie tickets. There is no sales tax to pay when one goes to the bowling alley. There is no sales tax on bingo tickets. Yet this Government is going to tax literally everything that moves in the country, and a lot of things that do not even move-tax, tax, tax.
Since this Conservative Government was elected there has never been in Canadian history as large a tax grab as has occurred in the last four and one-half years; never even during wartime when taxes were introduced for the war effort.
These people have gouged. They have ripped. They have dug in. They have pulled out more money from taxpayers. Oops, I should not say "taxpayers" because that implies the corporate sector as well, one sector that has been overlooked. There are still 60,000 large, profitable corporations that do not pay even a single penny in income tax. There are many that pay $1, $20 or $100, but there are 60,000 large, profitable corporations that do not even pay a single penny. That is the idea of conservative tax reform-no taxes on the wealthy, no taxes on the large corporations in many instances.
However, I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the small welding shop down the street, the person running a beauty salon up the street, and the person running a small cafe are all paying, they are all paying and paying and paying. For every Budget that is brought in they pay more, but this same privileged group, this group of 60,000 profitable corporations, does not even pay a penny, to say nothing at all of those which pay $1, $2 or $3. This is not a fair tax system, but a Conservative way to reduce the deficit.
There is another way. It is called the New Democrat way. It is where we start saying, for example, that one way to reduce the deficit is not to buy nuclear submarines-this Government is still going ahead with nuclear submarines-but to assist the forest industry where we can generate a great deal more. Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, that in the Throne Speech the forest industry is not even mentioned? Farmers and ranchers are not even mentioned. The mining industry is not even mentioned. Tourism is not even mentioned.

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. Riis
In other words, those of us who come from the regions of the country, which of course are most of us, are not mentioned in the Throne Speech. This is a Throne Speech again designed for central Canada, specifically Toronto. This has to change. Our idea as New Democrats is let us ask these profitable corporations to pay something, a minimum corporate tax. Let us abandon this nuclear submarine madness and save ourselves billions and billions of dollars. Let us put out some of these lush government contracts to tendering so that people will have a chance to tender. We could save hundreds of millions of dollars. But now the Government uses it to reward corporate pals. There is no tendering, Mr. Speaker, and this involves billions of dollars. It is amazing.
What was absent from the Throne Speech was any reference to the West Coast oil spill, the largest in North American history. There was some rhetoric about the environment.
I would like to conclude my remarks by moving a subamendment that reads as follows:
That the amendment be amended by adding the following words:
"and, specifically, that the House regrets the failure of the Government to provide adequate resources to deal with environmental crises and accidents; to regulate and enforce environmental laws; to monitor the state of our air, lands and waters; and to provide national standards of environmental protection".

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy my colleague's speeches in the House. He always throws figures around. I am not sure where he gets his facts and figures from. Most of the time when we look into them we find that they are very inadequate.
There are a couple of questions I want to ask. First, with respect to interest rates he said that he would lower interest rates in the country. If he were to lower interest rates in the country or to make regional interest rates as some of his colleagues have suggested, how would he stem the flow of capital out of those regions where there were low interest rates, which actually need the investment capital, to areas of the country where there are high interest rates? Or, how would he stem the flow of capital out of the country, chasing higher interest rates?
What is the NDP policy on that type of thing? How would it stop the flow of capital?
Second, how would the Hon. Member maintain inflation in the country? How would he stop the inflationary pressures that we are experiencing, not only in this country but in the other countries of the world? How would he have lower interest rates than his partners in the G-7, all of whom have been raising their interest rates lately because of the fear of inflation, because they do not want to go back to 1980 and 1981 when the Liberals sat back and let inflation run away? Then they had to give us extremely bitter medicine of some 22 per cent. That is the first thing I want to ask him.
The second question I would like him to cover is with respect to what he had to say about the sales tax. I do not think there is anyone in this country who would disagree that we need sales tax reform. Our domestic products are put at a disadvantage of some 25 per cent with those that they compete with from imports because of our outdated, outmoded manufacturing sales tax of 12 per cent.
Across the House I did not say music lessons. He knows I did not. I said "cars". There is a 12 per cent manufacturers' sales tax on automobiles today, on everything that is manufactured in this country, including bingo cards I might say.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

There is a 12 per cent tax on the printing of those bingo cards.
I want to ask him what he would do or what the NDP would do to reform this antiquated, outmoded, unproductive sales tax system. Would he do what his socialist friends did in New Zealand or Australia where they taxed food and everything else-everything-when they changed their tax system? What would the NDP do?

Not only will the cards be taxed, but just the ability to play will also be taxed.

As well as getting your hair cut, getting your eyes checked, your teeth fixed or your new suit, everything is going to be taxed, Mr. Speaker. I will come back to that.
April 7, 1989

First of all I will respond to the matter of interest rates. I do not know if Canadians are generally aware of the fact that real interest rates are higher than they have ever been in this entire decade. The real interest rate is the prime rate. We reduce the inflation factor to get the real interest rate. They are higher now than they were in 1980 through 1988.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
They are higher than at any time in this decade, with the exception of perhaps one month back in 1981. That is just a fact when we talk about high interest rates.
I must ask the Hon. Member why it is that our interest rates have to be so much higher than those in the United State. Not a single premier says that they need to be.
Let us assume that we can bring down our interest rates two or three percentage points to equal at least what they are in the United States. Why do I make this proposal? It is that if we reduce interest rates by 1 per cent, we cut the deficit and the debt significantly.
Our debt is large. I cannot sleep some night at night because I am reminded that the Conservatives have increased the debt on our children from $170 billion when they took office to over $320 billion today. They do not have a right to leave this kind of legacy to our children. Our debt has increased under this Government, and it is going up by billions of dollars a month. That is the reality. It is unbelievable. A lot of us have trouble sleeping because we are concerned about our children and our children's children.
By reducing interest rates one percentage point, we can really knock off billions of dollars from our debt repayment expectation.
What should we be doing when it comes to interest rates? We can drop them down one to three percentage points, again to bring us in line with the United States. We will also have a window of opportunity in July of this summer at the G-7 meeting to discuss a variety of things of mutual concern.
Why should our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) not put interest rates on that agenda and say: "let us work together to bring down these rates, in concert one with another"? He has not identified that as a priority for the next G-7 meeting in July, and I urge him to consider that.
The Address-Mr. DeBlois
The other question was on the sales tax. What the Minister of State for Privatization (Mr. McDermid) always forgets to ask me is my view on the 60,000 large profitable corporations that never pay any tax. He never asked me if I think this is a good idea.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We do not have 60,000.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is right, Mr. Speaker, we do not have 60,000 large profitable corporations. We have 60,219 large profitable corporations not paying a single penny in income tax. Maybe, if they were paying their fair share, we would not have to impose a national sales tax on children's clothing.
As we stand here today, there are $30 billion in deferred corporate taxes. If we just charged interest and did not ask them to pay back, there is $3 billion just like that. Then we would not have to ask to impose a special sales tax on children's stoiy books, pet foods and so on, but that is a priority of this Government. It wants to tax children's things and housing. I think I made my point.
I covered interest rates, inflation, and sales tax. What I also covered, Mr. Speaker, was what the Minister of Finance said-

I am quite prepared to reduce the level of economic activity in

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I return to my task in the House after several months of reflection and work in my constituency, and I would like to start by saying how happy I am that you, Mr. Speaker, and your team are still with us and offering you my full co-operation with the task at hand. I am pleased because a Member of Parliament, in addition to representing his riding, is also a member of a parliamentary body. The work we do here

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. DeBlois
in the House is an essential part of our task in general, because we not only have a duty to defend the interests of our constituencies but also to be aware of the national concerns of this great country of ours, from coast to coast.
I would like to start by saying how delighted I am that the Throne Speech read by the Governor General reflects our resolve to act on our election commitments, which include our commitment to protecting the environment, to the economy and to the neediest in our society whom we intend to continue to support, whatever Hon. Members opposite, the Liberals in the Official Opposition and the NDP, care to think.
Mr. Speaker, I found the following rather amusing. I read a lot of newspapers, as a former reporter. I noticed that a Liberal who was suggesting that those who are well off should not be given a pension, in order to help those who are disadvantaged, was quickly criticized by that protector of the needy and the poor, the Hon. Member for Laurier-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart). Let me explain. One of his colleagues, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-North (Mr. MacLaren) had dared to suggest that family allowances or old age pensions should not be paid to those people who are well off. So, the protector of the poor rose to say he was going to challenge that suggestion and fight it in caucus!
The Leader of the Official Opposition said in his one-hour speech, among other things: "We intend to remind the Government as often as necessary that Canada is not the private domain of the rich and the powerful, of the businessmen of this country. This country also belongs to people across Canada who cannot make ends meet." And we heard the usual emotional outpourings about the little guy and the unemployed. What a farce! I see that both Opposition Parties failed to take advantage of the period when the House was in recess to improve their thinking. After what happened during the free trade debate, I expected to meet with an Opposition that would show greater clarity and rigour in debate.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the Throne Speech is excellent in this respect. It is straightforward and responsible. For some years, because of the Liberal legacy, we have been saddled with an enormous deficit, and we shall have the fortitude to take the measures that are necessary to spare future generations the terrible burden
of a debt that is increasing every second, every minute and every hour of our existence in this country.
Some commentators and some Members opposite say that the Speech is just a lot of generalities without substance. Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote Michel Roy, one of the most respected editorial writers of this country, who wrote recently:
It is amazing to hear some commentators repeat over and over again that the Throne Speech is vague. Characteristically, however, inaugural speeches announce the broad directions a government intends to take, the philosophy that underlies its legislative program. And take note of this: "The terms of the Throne Speech leave no doubt as to this Government's commitment to a determined deficit reduction. In one sentence, the author of the speech perfectly illustrates how serious the present situation is: My Government is now borrowing money solely to pay the interest on previous borrowings".
It is therefore my view that everyone who listened to that speech in good faith could take note of this Government's will to do what previous governments had not done, namely to roll up their sleeves and to continue putting the brakes on the current deficit growth.
In that respect I am pleased to note the comments of an industrialist in my constituency who recently wrote to the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, who is taking surveys all around:
"Comments or suggestions to your Member of Parliament: 1. I hope that my M.P. stops playing Father Christmas." Of course, this was written before I was elected, Mr. Speaker.
"Stop playing Father Christmas with our money, cut altogether subsidies, especially to non-profit organizations and businesses who in the same country are making same products as non-subsidized firms."
2. "That my M.P. really tackles the elimination of the deficit."
So I think the mandate is quite clear, and this is but an example out of a thousand. People expect us to make an effort, they expect sacrifices. This is not easy, and I think everyone of us will have to pay the price. We have the will to be brave enough to go ahead and make sure public finance is put on a sounder basis.
April 7, 1989

So we are facing an opposition that is a bad loser bent on revenge. I was listening to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) who constantly suggests free trade, which we sold out to the United States, free trade means the end of our sovereignty, our Canadian way of doing things. I find that amusing, because Mr. Opposition Leader has Members in his caucus who are starting to see the light, although belatedly. Let me show you this headline-Marc Lalonde!-You heard of him? Marc Lalonde turns coat and becomes free trader! This is in Le Devoir of March 15, 1989.
Amusing! I find its never too late to see the light. With time, I think our friends opposite will finally understand. Two days ago in France Mr. Peterson, the Ontario Premier, applauded the merits of free trade in Europe, etc. Of course he said that abroad. Come now! Let's stop kidding the people! With time, we must come to realize that a majority of Canadians opted for much more direct and active trade with the United States.
As far as the New Democratic Party is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I heard the cassettes again. We just heard the Leader restate his defence of the poor and the oppressed. I think the resigning leader set matters straight when he very clearly stated on page 131 of Hansard of last Wednesday:
We are going to oppose with determined vigour every bill that
floors out of this Throne Speech and every budget item that will
come in the weeks ahead.
'talk of constructive opposition! Even before having seen anything, they will fight with determined vigour, not one but every bill, whatever. They will oppose for the sake of opposing.
I am a bit surprised. I would expect the Opposition to be constructive, positive. They could at least say: Let's wait and see. Who knows? The New Democratic Party says there might come up a bill to help the poor. But no! From the outset, they'll oppose every bill, all the gang of them.
Let me come to the core of my speech, Mr. Speaker. I would like to make two series of comments. The first one concerns the so-called Parliament holidays. For some time we have been hearing the Opposition suggest we had been sitting in our constituencies for six months. We were not putting the House to work. It's like saying MPs were just sitting on their behinds. I for one can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that since the end of the Christmas holidays, I have been in my constituency's office every day. I have my office diary here. I challenge any Member in this House to come and see in my diary what I have been doing for three months.
The Address-Mr. DeBlois
Also on this subject, I heard the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Mills) just give this very gripping testimony about his little daughter who was humiliated in school because people started to laugh when she said that her father was a Member of Parliament. I understand them, those young people. And part of it is that some journalists on Parliament Hill never stopped talking about "holidays".
Recently, Mr. Speaker, on the opening of the House, we saw in The Citizen, "Commons holiday ends".
We saw others. Here is Mr. Weston:

"MP's old and new are in a particularly scrappy mood after their 14-week parliamentary break".

I am not in a scrappy mood. I am in great shape and it is not because I have just been on vacation, believe me.
Mr. MacGillivray says here:

"The Members could use the extra weeks because they had been put to work so quickly after the November 21 election".

Another one says here:

"The three months that Parliament has not been sitting has in simple terms cost taxpayers $50 million to staff and maintain the empty Chamber and mostly empty Members' offices".

What a disgrace! Like the employees in my riding office. I have had five for the past three months. I am not afraid to name them: Claude Beauchamp, Ginette Hupe, Marie Garneau, Lisette Harvey and Solange Veilleux. When these people saw that, these people who were paid for three months, who worked day and night in my riding office, they were literally insulted.
I sort of get the feeling sometimes that Parliamentary reporters here on the Hill deal with national subjects. I know, because I was a parliamentary correspondent at the National Assembly. What interests them is the big national issues: sales tax, submarines. But what we do in our ridings, the ordinary backbenchers, does not interest them. None of them comes to our ridings to see what we do. I find that absolutely shameful; I find that shocking.

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. DeBlois
And, Mr. Speaker, you know my love for Latin quotations. Do they come to my mind? The ancients said, De minimis non curat praetor. It means that the magistrate does not care about minor details. Some journalists on Parliament Hill do not care about the small fry-the MP in his riding. That does not interest them. For them, it is nuclear issues, nuclear submarines, privatization. What we do in our constituencies does not interest them.
I think of a guy like Michel Vastel. He is not a bad fellow, he writes a lot and works hard. I find him interesting at times, and he wrote this, "The House of Commons costs us $190 million this year, of which $105 million is for the Members of Parliament alone. However, they are not paid just to attend their constituents' funerals and weddings or to look after social security cheques, although these duties are important. What Mr. Mulroney is doing is an affront to parliamentary democracy".
Well look, do these people live in the clouds? I know, I was a parliamentary reporter in Quebec City and it was dull when the legislature was not sitting. People not doing investigative journalism who want official news. .. the House is not sitting, there are no press conferences. They have nothing to give their boss. The boss asks them, "What report are you doing for me tonight?". But nothing has happened. The House is not sitting. So what these people should normally. . . and I am not accusing all journalists, Mr. Speaker. There are some excellent ones, thank God!
But some of them distort the facts and lead people to believe that when we are not in the House, we are on vacation or travelling. We are having fun, whatever. Well, I think it is time for the people listening to us to know what a Member who wants to take his constituency work seriously does! And I am not the only one, many... I just mentioned the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood who went to Quebec City for three weeks to learn French. I congratulate him, even though he is an opponent. He used those three months to learn the countiy's other official language. If all Anglophones had the courage to do that, I would be really proud. I went to Toronto for a week to start to learn English, to improve, and I will be happy on the day I can tell you what I think in English.
But that being said, it was not a waste of time. I think it is one of the great benefits of the House of Commons to provide all Members and their spouses with the opportunity to improve their ability in the second language. I worked on it, I was not loafing by going to Toronto to study English. From nine in the morning till nine in the evening, I was with teachers and I was there to learn. Yes, thank you, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the words used by the Hon. Member opposite are not unparliamentary. He has repeated them twice.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: This kind of language should not be used. Although I do not think it has led to any disorder, I would ask the Hon. Member to refrain from using it.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your comment, and I will be careful not to use this kind of language. You will understand that in the heat of debate and especially with such attentive listeners, I might sometimes express myself by using images which are in common use in my region. This might seem trivial, but when ordinary people speak loud and clear, they use images of that kind. I have not invented them, I have just picked them up. And I respect these people even if they do not always use the language of Shakespeare or the sophisticated language of certain intellectuals.
Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, I am proud to report on what I have done. Let me say, for example, that in the past three months, I have opened 325 files involving my constituents. I am extremely proud to say that I have spoken with all the people in the riding of Montmorency who have phoned me or come to visit me in my constituency office. In this way, I have helped 188 individuals about such things as employment assistance, tax problems, old age pensions, unemployment insurance, housing. Private businessmen also come to me to get information about federal programs. I have been in touch with public servants on their behalf. Furthermore, representatives from 88 non profit organizations have come to see me about federal programs in such areas as employment and immigration, housing, community affairs, and so on. And then there are municipal matters. Half a dozen mayors from my riding have come to see me.
April 7, 1989

Add to all this, Mr. Speaker, the preparation of my householder, which is a source of great pride for me. With this publication, I have done a survey in my riding. Gentlemen opposite may laugh. Some find it amusing when we consult the people. For my part, I am very proud to do so. I conducted a poll on the abortion issue. Instead of making lofty speeches, instead of holding forth, instead of blathering as some of my friends opposite are doing, I went to hear what the people of my riding had to say, I got some mail and at the appropriate time and place I will know what to say to convey the feelings of my constituents.
In spite of all that, Mr. Speaker, I did have an opportunity to be away from my riding for a couple of weeks to represent my country on the United Nations Commission on Human Rights-one of my Liberal opponents was even a member of our party-where I had a close look at the leading role Canada is playing to uphold and promote human rights.
Hopefully, Mr. Speaker, this information will enlighten my colleagues in the House. I should think we all agree on that score and that most of us take advantage of these parliamentary recesses to be close to our relatives and our constituents.
A second point, Mr. Speaker, and I will conclude my remarks. As a Quebecer I can tell you that I felt insulted by the words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) concerning Premier Bourassa of Quebec. My speech this afternoon gives me an opportunity to say that I am at one with the Quebec Premier who knows the importance of protecting the rights and the French fact in this country.
Once again, of course, Premier Bourassa had to invoke the notwithstanding clause. He did not have much choice because the Constitution foisted on us by the Liberals prevented Quebec from joining the Constitution. If we want to promote French as we are cleared to do by the Supreme Court, we have to be practical and pragmatic, and in that respect I am certainly not going to blame the Premier of Quebec-brothers as we are through race and culture-for taking steps to enhance the promotion of French within the huge Anglophone majority in Canada and in the United States. As a matter of fact, a number of the Liberal colleagues of the Leader of the Opposition-and I understand there will soon be a leadership convention-including the Hon. Member for Laurier-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre), or people like Francis
The Address-Mr. DeBlois
Fox and other former MPs, have all said: We lost our roots in Quebec during the last election. Mr. Turner's speech was just the way again to sink your roots in Quebec. I am ashamed about the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition, and in that context I am proud of the remarks of my leader the Prime Minister and of the Speech from the Throne.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of asking the Hon. Member what he will be sitting on in coming weeks, as undoubtedly you will be glad to hear. Among other things, I am pleased to learn that he sent a householder, an excellent news, and I commend him for sharing his experience with the House of Commons.
I want to get back to some of the remarks he made in his speech. He said the Opposition had not been constructive enough, and he blamed the Leader of the Official Opposition and the leader of the New Democratic Party for taking a negative approach with respect to his Government. According to him we should be a lot more constructive, even when the Government does not act properly, which is the case presently.
I should like to ask my colleague opposite if one can conclude that he thought the Conservative Opposition was constructive during the many years they were on this side, particularly under the "leadership" of one Eric Nielsen who was acting Leader of the Opposition for a number of years while waiting for the present leader to find a riding somewhere so he would have a seat in the House of Commons. Specifically I should like to ask him whether he agreed with the attitude of some Members who at one time were prepared to chain themselves to the clerk's table to protest against a legislative measure, or whether he did not see anything wrong with the other incident one night when Conservative Members-led by the Hon. Member for Calgary who is now a Minister of the Crown-decided to surround the chair of the Speaker of the House of Commons.
I wonder whether he approves of that kind of thing or of the pairing system we used to have in the past when an Opposition Member and a Government Member had to leave the country together with a parliamentary delegation. Conservative Members broke the agreement, they sneaked out of their beds in Europe in the middle of the night to catch a Concorde flight and fly back early in the morning in an attempt to defeat the Government. Is that what my colleague on the other side calls constructive opposition?

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. DeBlois

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, obviously, I appreciate the historical knowledge of the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). Of course I do not live in the past. How should I put it? I am not a blindly partisan Member of Parliament and I do not support anything that might have been done, on any side of the House, against any positive position in this Chamber. You can keep harping on some past history, but I will not lose any sleep over it. I am here in 1989; I was not here ten years ago. From now on, personally, when it is a matter of programs, of official languages, I think I shall try to contribute as positively as I can to the debate and I hope that the Opposition will be able to give us positive arguments, whatever their limitations and the constraints they are under.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Hon. Member for Montmorency-Orleans (Mr. DeBlois) and I would like to ask him a question because it occurred to me that maybe something had been forgotten in his speech. He was talking about the deficit and the burden his Government inherited from the Liberal Government in 1984. Mr. Speaker, my question to the Hon. Member is: Does he know what the deficit was in 1984 and does he know what the deficit is now, after four years of Conservative Government?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

What was the national debt in 1984, not in 1960? What was the national debt in 1984 and where is it today?

speechtext:

speechtext:
In
rising for debate on the Throne Speech, I must change gears. Normally the opening days of a session on the Throne Speech are akin to spring training in baseball. You are there to warm up the arm, get your pitchers in place, get your legs in shape, and begin preparing for the real competition. The real battle will begin once you head into the major leagues.
Unfortunately in this debate, a disturbing, disquieting element has been introduced. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spoke yesterday on his view of the Constitution, his attitude toward the protection of rights in this country. No Canadian and no Member of Parliament can let lie the assertions and the derogation of prime ministerial responsibility that we heard yesterday. We cannot allow a statement of that sort to lie without a response. It would be the first time in the history of this country that the First Minister of this nation, charged with the responsibility of being the protector of the fundamental laws of this land, describes them as being worthless. It is incredible and beyond belief that the steward who is responsible for giving inspiration to school children, men and women, and to all citizens about respect for the law, about an acceptance and a toleration for the constitutional framework that we have, can be so cavalier and callous in his dismissal of it. It is a remarkable and unprecedented intervention by the Prime Minister of this country. I hope we will never see it again.
The Prime Minister has done a great disservice to all Canadians for purely crass, political, partisan reasons. He has regurgitated that strange streak of revenge that is embodied in his soul in an effort to get back at the previous Prime Minister and the Liberals. He has to wreak his bile on somebody, so he tries to regurgitate history by saying Mr. Trudeau and the Liberals were responsible for some of the impasses that we now have in the constitutional development of this country. The fact that the Prime Minister will twist, turn, and distort history does not bother him a bit.
That type of assertion has been false and is irresponsible. I think all Members of Parliament should use this
The Address-Mr. Axworthy
opportunity of the Throne Speech to remind the Prime Minister of his solemn oath of office, which is to defend the laws of this country, not to break them down and crash them to bits.
I want to take issue with the assertion the Prime Minister made. He attempted to demonstrate that the Government of which I was a member was itself responsible for undermining national unity by introducing and passing in this Parliament the ratification of the new Constitution in 1981 and 1982. What an incredible, silly, stupid assertion to make.
As the Prime Minister well knows, that was an historical moment. One of the great attributes of great politicians, of which he is not, is to seize the moment. Fortunately, we had a Prime Minister who understood how to seize the moment. Mr. Trudeau saw that convergence of events, that may not occur in this country for another 100 years, come together with a change to repatriate and restore our Constitution into Canadian control and to provide Canadians with a Charter of Rights that has become one of the most important documents in the history of Canada.
If you read the legal, judicial and constitutional experts, they say that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms reflects the new reality of Canada. It reflects the new rights, powers and privileges that have been denied women for so long. It gives expression to the multicultural character of this country. This is a document written in the 1980s, not 100 years ago. It gives expression to a new sense of rights of aboriginal people that have been denied for so long. Each of the articles in that charter are now in front of the courts across this country. They are being tested by lawyers to demonstrate how we can broaden, expand, elaborate and shape the law. To say the Constitution means nothing, that it is not worth the paper it is written on, is a total denial of what is taking place in a dynamic and effervescent way in this country. In Family Courts, Juvenile Courts or Supreme Courts of this country, cases are being heard based upon that Charter.
The Prime Minister says that because we had to agree to the "notwithstanding clause" somehow the Constitution is worthless. Well, I say to you for all the many Canadians who feel that the Charter is their endowment and the ratification of their rightful place in Canadian society, the words of the Prime Minister will sound hollow and sour in their ears.
Mr. Speaker, even on the notwithstanding clause, let us look at a little bit of the history. I do not want to regurgitate but I want to say something very clearly.

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. Axworthy
There was one reason only why the previous Liberal Government accepted a notwithstanding clause. That was because Premiers of provinces, including Conservative Premiers-the Sterling Lyons and the Peter Lougheeds of this world-would not allow any constitutional development to take place unless they got that clause. It was an expression of that virulent provincialism that is so much alive in this country today, where we are fragmenting the country into pieces. That is the reason.
There was nothing in the original proposal by the Liberal Government, by Mr. Trudeau, by Mr. Chretien, by the Cabinet of the country, by the Parliamentary assembly. It was clearly an unequivocal condition of approval heaped upon us by a group of provincial Premiers, who have a very different concept of Canada and a very different view of how this country should be governed. They did not believe in the supremacy of the individual and that at the base of all law should be individual rights. They said no. The collective rights of a provincial majority in our assemblies takes precedence.
I understand that. That is, in a sense, the traditional kind of Conservative theology. It represents that societies are organized around groups, regions or collectivities, not around individuals. He was joined by the New Democratic Premier of Saskatchewan who shared that view. That is why we are so different from the other two parties. It is because we have put as the basic premise of everything the sacred democracy, the right of the individual. But that was challenged by provincial Premiers.
The Hon. Member for Lethbridge (Mr. Thacker) laughs about that.

from us our own example of that kind of re-interpretation of fundamental fact.
The important point is not who was responsible. What is important is that it is there and it has been used in a way to suppress individual rights. Surely that is the real lesson that has to be learned. Surely the responsibility is not upon the Government of Canada to change that. The fact of the matter is that when the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) had that opportunity behind the closed doors of Meech Lake, he did not use it. He did not even bother to raise it.

speechtext:
That is right! At that time I did not hear the Prime Minister saying anything about that when he came before the House of Commons. We listened very carefully when he spoke about his Constitutional proposals. I heard nothing about the notwithstanding clause. Liberals raised it. Our Justice critic raised it. Our Leader raised it and said that should be part of the package. We introduced it as part of the amendments. I ask this: it is not too difficult a question. Even a Conservative Member of Parliament could understand it. If it was such a big problem, if it was such a terrible sin, if it was such a horrible smirch on the honour of Canada, then when we brought in the amendment why did not the Prime Minister and his colleagues agree to it? Why did they vote against it? It would not have been hard to do.
I listened to the Prime Minister yesterday and today he was in high dudgeon. High dudgeon is okay after the fact. But when he had the chance, where was he? I know where he was. I know where the Prime Minister was. He was not dealing with it at that point because he was trying to make a deal.
We see it as a problem, Mr. Speaker. We want it changed. We think it is very important for the operation of federalism to make that change. When our Leader spoke in the Throne Speech debate, again it was a question of trying to solicit from the Prime Minister a clear statement, not a high roll of anger but a clear statement.
My colleagues and I remember very well the period of this assembly just before Christmas when the issue emerged because of the Premier of Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause. We had the then Secretary of State sneaking behind the curtains rushing out to give little press conferences for the Quebec press saying he thought it was a good idea while the Prime Minister was in here saying he did not think it was a good idea. We could never get the two of them to agree as to who was right. The only good thing I can say about having the present Minister of the Environment (Mr. L. Bouchard)
April 7, 1989

in his existing portfolio is that he is no longer the Secretary of State. He is no longer responsible for defending minority rights. What a paltry record he had in that position.
The Conservatives are the Government and we want to know. Even after all this time it is hard for them to recognize their responsibilities. When you start out not believing in Government, it is kind of hard to recognize its importance. But the Conservatives are in Government and they must take responsibility. It is pretty easy to end this debate. All the Prime Minister has to do is say "Okay, let us get this House of Commons together and come to an agreement on how we get rid of this clause". He does not have to dance around in his Gucci shoes. He does not have to jump up and down in anger and push and shove and yell and scream. All he has to do is say "Let us get the Commons together and do it". We are on side. The New Democrats are on side. I say to the Prime Minister wherever he may be, whichever watering hole he may be in at this moment, let him sort of decide what he is prepared to do.

Before I conclude, I think it is also important that this kind of shell game come to an end. I thought after getting a second mandate we would have a somewhat different kind of Prime Minister. I thought maybe we would get someone a little more honest and straightforward. He is now a world's statesman. He has turned the Government of Canada into a travel agency to arrange his world tours. I thought maybe this time we would get things a little more in order and that when we got the Throne Speech maybe we would get some straight facts. Again, I listened to the speech yesterday. Was it a whopper. You should have heard the things the Prime Minister was saying, Mr. Speaker, about why the economy was going wrong and why we have to get the deficit down.
The Address-Mr. Axworthy
I had the occasion to pick out a speech that was given by the present Prime Minister when he was Leader of the Opposition. It is fascinating to note what he said in 1984 and what he is saying now. In 1984 he said that "one of the reasons this Liberal Government is so terrible is that there is a flight of capital from Canada. That is what is driving interest rates up". He went on to say, "There is a flight of job creating capital". He said $17 billion has left the country. "As a result, this huge equity outflow is forcing the dollar down and interest rates up and we must do something about it".
Is it not true that last year some $30 billion left Canada? It is almost double under the Tory regime as to what it was under the Liberal regime. I did not hear the Prime Minister talk of that. I did not hear him talking about the reason for the flight of capital is because he has lost control over the whole question of foreign investment.
Then we come to the great matter of the deficit. Was he mad in 1984. You should have heard him. "Those Liberals, and the debt has reached $180 million". That is what he said as the Tory Leader of the Opposition in 1984. In 1988, it is $340 billion. As long as this this debtor's spiral continues, long-term interest rates will not be coming down. What was true in 1984 is true in 1988, and we had better do something about it. I did not hear the Prime Minister attribute those types of causes.
Here is an another titbit. This is the Prime Minister of research and development. He is the one who states that high technology is going to make the day. Back in 1984 he stated that the present rate of spending was terrible because only 1.3 per cent of GDP was spent on R and D. After five years of Conservative Government, it is now
1.2	per cent. We are even falling behind.
When one looks at the cut-backs in all the departments, one has to ask where was the Prime Minister when he should have been reading his 1984 speeches? I am going to send this speech to him, Mr. Speaker. This would be an awfully good speech for 1988. We only have to upgrade those figures. We only have to double the figures on the deficit, double the figures on the interest rates, and send him the speech. The only problems are his solutions, and that is where we always come a little bit of a cropper.
Tories are not very good at solutions. They do not know how to use Government very well. They do not have an understanding of the public sector. They do not have a sense of its capacity or ability to serve Canadians. We know how the Government serves its friends, but we are not so sure how it serves the rest of the country, which represents 99.9 per cent.

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. Axworthy
Unfortunately, when one refers to the Throne Speech, I guess we can say that the masquerade is over. The charade has come to an end. We no longer have those Tories talking about themselves as being Progressive Conservatives. Now we have the real agenda. Now we have the hard-rock, neo-conservative, put-it-to-them, jackboot philosophy that we knew was there all the time.
We have a Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) who in her brief tenure in office has made Margaret Thatcher look like Mother Theresa in terms of compassion and caring. We have a Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) who drops so many messes that I feel I should take a newspaper into the House and swat him on the nose every day to clean up those messes. He does not have an understanding of his portfolio.
The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), the highly respected senior statesman of the party, is now hiding behind the desk because his brave promises of saving VIA Rail for western Canada are now going on the cutting room floor of the Treasury Board. The Government is betraying itself.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty) has finally climbed out of his bathtub and is now preparing to do the same in the health and welfare field that he did in the area of defence, that is, to resurrect the cold war. This time it is not a cold war against Russia. It is going to be a cold war against poor people, aging people, and all those others who look toward Government for some kind of survival.
I tried to find a way of describing the Throne Speech. My vocabulary was not sufficient. I went to the new Oxford Dictionary and found the interesting word "entropy". It means lack of judgment, lack of guidance, chaos, no planning, no direction, no path. That is a good way of describing what we have. However, underneath it is that mean-spirited sense that the Government is not there to try to provide a sense of direction, a feeling amongst Canadians that they can rely upon a Government that will respond. There is a sense of a Government that carries a blind eye to the reality of the world. It does not care about the takeovers, acquisitions, and restructuring of our economy. It gives two lines to foreign policy. There are enormous things happening in the world. Disarmament and arms control are becoming one of the great opportunities of our time.
I spent a little time becoming acquainted with the area of international trade. The Government talks about our
new opportunities in Europe and Asia. The Free Trade Agreement with the United States gets a passing mention. Now the Government is talking about Europe and Asia and how we are going to do great things there. It does not mention that in the last couple of years it has cut back all the expenditures on trade development, trade promotion, and trade fairs.
Our current accounts are falling. In 1985 we had a $900 million surplus with the United Kingdom. Now it is a $3.1 billion deficit. In 1985 we had a $327 million surplus with European trading companies. Now it is a $4 billion deficit. We are falling behind in every area of the world. At the same time, the Government is cutting expenditures to help small and medium-sized business to provide promotion and development of trade opportunities around the world.
Once again this document is exposed as being a totally fallacious accounting. It does not deal with reality. It deals with the fact that the Government is going to squeeze, pummel, and inflict pain upon the Canadian people for its own incompetence, mismanagement, and flagrancy. The message of the Throne Speech is that someone has to pay the price for Tory incompetence. The Official Opposition will not let the Government get away without telling the people of Canada exactly what is going on in the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to be taking part in the debate on the Speech from the Throne, as it is a privilege to sit in this House. Our debate here centres around Canada's obvious problems, around our national goals, around the Government agenda and the future.
April 7, 1989

The Throne Speech touched on many areas but those which impressed me most were, first, the crying need for fiscal responsibility in the country, to really tackle our budget deficit and our national debt. I was also struck by the words of caring about the environment in the Throne Speech. I thought that was really a pivotal part in it. Perhaps this is our greatest responsibility to the future. I was certainly struck as well by comments on reforming the tax system. I think that Canadians really want us to work toward a fairer tax system in general.
Before I comment on some of those areas, I would like to say a couple of words about politics and partisanship. Some issues are simply too important for politics and for party positions. For example, I think environmental concerns should rise above politics. I also think that in many ways economics should rise above politics. In both of these instances we are talking about something fragile and wonderful, that is, the future. For example, if we poison our waters, pollute our air, our soil and our earth, then it is those who come after us who will really suffer. It is the same with our economy. If we indebt our land, if we bankrupt our children, the same will happen. If we indebt ourselves to foreign lenders, then it is not our generation that suffers immediately, but the generations which come after us.
These are clearly not Conservative problems, nor Liberal problems. They are not New Democratic problems. They are all of our problems. I think the Speech from the Throne indicated that the government is going to make reducing the deficit a national priority, and I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I stand 100 per cent behind that objective. I feel the Minister of Finance is most responsible in throwing every effort into cutting down the amount we are forced to borrow to run Canada.
Politicians have been too reluctant to talk about our finances. Maybe some of them do not understand. Maybe some of them do not care. Maybe others thought Canadians were not concerned about who pays the bills and how. Maybe the polsters told the politicians that talk about deficits is not sexy with taxpayers, and so politicians have not really been talking about Canada's dirty little economic secret, but it is clearly too late to pretend that it does not exist.
We have a national debt of $325 billion. Every year it costs us close to $30 billion just to pay the interest on that existing debt. Now the taxes that Canada collects are basically enough to support the expenditures that the government makes, but we do not have close to the $30
The Address-Mr. G. Turner
billion it that it takes to service that debt. So we borrow it, and every year that we borrow, our debt increases that much further. That is why we have a deficit. It is the interest payment on the debt.
It means every hour, every day, our country falls deeper into debt, and during the few minutes I am going to be standing here, Canada will fall into debt by another $1 million. Today alone, Friday, April 7, our country will be $18 million more indebted than it was at the end of the day yesterday. At the end of this year, our country will be thirty thousand million dollars more in debt than it was last year.
If we ran a business that way, the business would be bankrupt. If your family handled its finances that way, the family would be insolvent, homeless and penniless, and yet here is Canada living on borrowed money and borrowed time, and only now have we really started to talk about getting it back on track.
So I say that it is not a partisan problem. It is simply a tragic problem that we all need to address. I do not think that Canada should run deficits, and I do not think that deficits are anything more than deferred taxation. Deferred from where? Well, from future generations. Deficits are the economic equivalent of toxic pollution of the environment. They are like cutting down rain forests, like polluting water, like pumping sulphur into the atmosphere.
Deficits are irresponsible because they pollute the future. Deficits bring debt, and debt will kill Canada. It is just that simple. Debt will impair our ability to set our own interest rates for example. Debt will ensure that taxes will forever rise, and the middle class as a result will slowly be wiped out. Debts also put our social programs at risk. These deficits that we are running simply represent a transfer of wealth from one generation to the next, from the future generation to ours.
As the Finance Minister has said, it is time to be building for the future and not borrowing from it. So what are we going to do about it?
The Speech from the Throne started to pave the way, and that is why I support it. It paves the way for the Finance Minister to bring in a budget on April 27, which will be responsible and tough and which will do the right things. Doubtless there will be special interest groups and critics who will howl on budget night. But I would like to ask, who among us would be Finance Minister on that night? Who has the courage to stand up and tell Canadians what to do? It takes guts for a politician to do that. It takes guts for a politician to promise people less instead of incessantly promising them more. It takes guts to stand here and tell Canadians they have to make

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. G. Turner
sacrifices, when life seems good and credit at the bank is easy to get, but it has got to be done. There is no choice.
Everyone is saying it. For example, the Chamber of Commerce did a survey the other day that found that only 9 per cent of Canadian businesses thought the Government had done enough to reduce the deficit. The International Monetary Fund, as we know, wants our Government to cut the deficit by $9 billion. If it does not, it warns that we are going to be incurring deficits well above $30 billion for quite some time.
Editorial writers from across the country have been urging the government to do something about it, do more, cut further, be more responsible. Business groups have been there at the bar urging us as well, and I will quote from a speech given the other day by the President of the Business Council for National Issues:
Interest payments on the national debt today add up to more than twice what is spent on our major elderly benefit programs combined. Old Age Security, Guaranteed Income Supplements and Spouse Allowances are three times more than the federal government spends on all economic and regional development programs. Even more worrisome is the prospect of recession, saddled with large deficits and soaring debts of servicing costs, the capacity of the country to respond to a significant economic slow-down is alarmingly limited.
Yes, those are voices from the business community, voices of people who have studied the economics of the situation and who are frankly concerned about it, but the business people are not standing alone. Standing shoulder to shoulder with them are legions of ordinary people.
Over the last few days, Mr. Speaker, my office has been swamped with hundreds of letters from individual Canadians who are concerned about the defict and who want a strong message related to the Finance Minister.
I would like to quote just a couple of comments that have come in.
Linda Adshead of Mississauga, Ontario writes me:
During the last federal election, my two major concerns were the deficit and the future of our environment. I feel that if we do not get these things under control, we will not have a country to worry about. The deficit has been a concern of mine for many years. It is now out of control, and something has to be done about it now.
Pat Kenler of Whitby, Ontario writes me:
The massive debt which the people of this country must support is overwhelming. When the budget is brought down in April, drastic spending cut-backs must be enforced. I am truly concerned about my future as a Canadian. I agree we should promote patriotism where Canadians should stop bitching about what the government does for them. We are in a country so vast, so full of resources that there is opportunity for everyone. Please cut back on all the money that is handed to people to get their vote.
Helen Gordon of Mono Mills, Ontario writes me:
The situation is as grave as the great depression. What should be done? First of all, action by all citizens, politicians, corporations, bureaucrats. Governments must reduce spending. Citizens will have to pay more taxes as do corporations. Lobbyists will have to reduce, if not eliminate, grandiose ideas of government grants for everything. Citizens will have to realize they cannot have it all. National support programs will have to be monitored and reduced to within operable range. Full co-operation from all aspects of society demands a tough attitude. This will not be easy. We have had it that way for too long. The time of decision is at hand.
Mrs. Penny of Mississauga, Ontario writes me:
I have reached the age of 60 and have watched with dismay our ever increasing spending and consequent debt. Everyone has been paid too much and lived beyond their means for the past 30 years. Shame and thrift used to be two very important words. We used to brag about how little we pay for something. Now all of us brag about how much we pay.
The Gaylord family of Campbellville, Ontario write me:
Mr. TUmer, we are prepared to help where we can. At J.F. Kennedy's exhortation is needed as a philosophy: "Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country."
Help us convince the majority in government that we need to reduce the deficit, that spending reductions are essential, that social programs need to be reviewed.
Lynn Schnitter of Stroud, Ontario, writes me:
I have read what you have written on the deficit. I looked at our five-year old son and I realized I must write to you now.
You see, I don't want our son growing up in a banana republic, nor do I want him to be part of a future USA north. We are trying hard to provide him with the financial security for our future and we are certainly not counting on our Canada pension for ourselves. We have swallowed personal sacrifices in the past and present and would do so again for the economic well-being not only of ourselves but for our country.
These are the voices of the people. It is not big business, not partisans, not politicians, just people. They know that deficits breed high interest rates. The people know that all we get is a vicious circle of more debt which threatens people further. It threatens their families, threatens their jobs and threatens our whole future.
April 7, 1989

We have a situation now that if deficits are not trimmed and debt is not refinanced, we will simply lose the ability to set our own interest rate policy. That will mean that homeownership will slip through the fingers of more and more Canadians as mortgage rates rise unchecked. It will make it harder for people to afford consumer and durable goods. That will ultimately result in the loss of jobs for thousands of Canadians. How long will we allow this to keep on?
Can we not say on April 27, when the Budget is brought in, that this is where Canada stands, this is where Canada says enough, from here on we manage events, we pay our own way. We are honest, we are upfront. We tell people what comes next. We ask for fairness for all. I think we can do it.
Between Confederation and Canada's Centennial in 1967, the country ran up $28 billion in debt. For that we built a transcontinental railway, we fought and won two world wars. But in the next 21 years we increased the national debt by 1,000 per cent, to the point where now we are one of the most indebted peoples on the face of the earth. At this rate it is only a matter of time before our whole national economy is threatened and we lose the ability to finance medicare, social programs, health, education, and all the rest for which we have fought so hard.
Obviously in a situation like this the Government needs the help of everyone. In particular, the country needs the help of those of us in the House.
I listened to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty) this morning trying to make a similar point, that all of us share the responsibility for getting the country back on track. All of us know that the ultimate threat we faced to our spending programs is $30 billion a year in additional borrowing. That one thought alone should bring us above the partisan frame, and I hope it does.
The problem can only be solved if we act as responsible individuals, especially here. Instead of simply dumping by rote upon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on April 27, it is my hope that all the words that are spoken in response to what he does are constructive and designed to help Canada. Nobody wants more taxes, especially me. I am probably one of the few Members of the House who has had the privilege in the past to be outside waving a sign in front of this Parliament, talking about exactly this, the issue of taxation. What we face now is a war for Canada's future. What the Throne Speech tells us is that we have a duty, simply, clearly, responsibly, to take action.
The Address-Mr. G. Turner
I would rather see billions of dollars more spent every year on caring for my parents in their old age, or caring for the environment for our children, than I would see those billions go to foreign lenders in Tokyo and New York.
My seat here in the House of Commons falls on an imaginary line running between government members and opposition Members. My greatest hope is that during this session we can reach across the imaginary lines, lay down the rhetoric, and do something right for Canada.

If he is to cut the social programs, does that mean he would tell not only the House but the caucus and his Ministers that he is not in favour of the universality of the programs we have now with regard to family allowances, old age pensions and medicare? Mr. Speaker, I support a progressive tax system which effectively takes from those who do not require social assistance programs and social assistance payments, and returns it to the federal treasury. I think that is the fairest way of dealing with the situation at this particular time.
As far as the nuclear submarine program is concerned, the Government has a plan by which over the course of the next 25 years annual expenditures are roughly $300 million will be expended to finance the construction of the submarines. Certainly the defence policy White Paper clearly defines the need. If we do make the argument and believe that we should defend Canada, it clearly stated that that was the most effective way of doing it.
I think we must go beyond merely looking at that expenditure because the cuts that will be required for the additional revenues will be in the area of $5 billion to $7 billion. We need to go much further than that program.

Yet my observation in the last four or five years, while we were running up the first $38 billion annual deficit which the Conservative Government shared with the previous Liberal Government, followed by a series of $30 billion plus deficits, is that interest rates actually dropped because we permitted the Canadian dollar to drop. When we had a 68-cent dollar, we had relatively low interest rates. The Government, for some reason, seems to be instructing the-

If the Hon. Member will check, he will find that the interest rates have gone up nearly 4 per cent at a time when the dollar has gone up from 68 to about 83 or 84 cents.
The reason I raise it is that it seems the data do not fit with the theory generally abroad that deficits cause rising interest rates, and this is important for deficit cutters like the Hon. Member for Halton-Peel (Mr. Turner), because when the interest rate is kept down, that means that there is less cost in servicing that deficit. If we would go from a 12 per cent to an 8 per cent interest rate, for instance, rather than paying just over $30 billion a year in financing costs, that would drop to $20 billion and there would be an additional $10 billion for discretionary spending, or perhaps even a reduction of the accumulated deficit.
I was just wondering where the Hon. Member's analysis goes in that regard. Low interest rates and low dollars permit this country to continue to be a very valuable exporter and encourage the exports that helped us to maintain particularly the hinterland regions like mine.
