Mr. Speaker, I am also pleased to respond to that question, and I think it is well put by the Hon. Member.
In terms of interest rates, it would be clearly impossible for the Government to instruct the Bank of Canada merely to cause an across the board reduction in interest rates. That would simply send a negative signal to world markets and would result in a drop in our currency.
Ultimately, that would accelerate the problem by forcing us to re-examine our interest rate policy in order to rescue our currency. So I do not think that is an alternative.
I am sure the Hon. Member knows quite well the theory of supply and demand. When there is a great demand for a commodity, the price of it goes up. Simply put, the price of money is interest, and when there is great demand for the commodity of money, the price of money goes up. When a Government puts great demands on the capital markets, as a result we have competition for available funds and we do see interest rates rise as a result of that.
There is another element coming into play, of course. We do have an inflationary problem in Canada, particularly in central Canada. It is important for us to address and deal with that problem early on before it accelerates. We are in an economic situation now not unlike that of the late 1970s. It is important for us to put the brakes on the economy slowly, responsibly, before it runs away, and we have an inflation problem that takes double-digit interest rates to deal with. An ounce of cure now is much better than a pound of prevention later, and I fully support the Bank of Canada's policy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this afternoon to take part in the debate on the second Throne Speech of the Thirty-Fourth Parliament. Some people may assume we are talking about the inaugural speech, Mr. Speaker, but that is not the case. In fact, we had a very short session before Christmas to accommodate the agreement negotiated by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) and his U.S. counterpart, the President of the United States.
I must say that I regret the outcome of the first session. I regret that the Canadian Government, despite our efforts to convince them that they were on the wrong track, nevertheless decided to ratify this Free Trade Agreement which in both the short and long term will be harmful to Canada's economy.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by taking this opportunity to thank the people of the riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell for their tremendous support during the last election campaign. I am particularly thankful, Mr. Speaker, that my constituents decided to ask me to sit for a second term in this Chamber, and that they did so by giving me a vast majority, nearly 26,000 votes more than my nearest opponent. I am very thankful, and hope that during the next four or five years, I will be able to fulfil the duties attached to a mandate I was given with such an impressive majority.

The riding that I represent is indeed a very special one. I am sure that each MP thinks that the constituency he or she represents is the nicest, and it is after the one that I represent. We are probably all correct, of course.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, Glengarry, of course, is the home of the first Premier of the Province of Ontario, Sir John Sandfield MacDonald. It is also the birthplace of the United Empire Loyalist movement, and it is, of course, a very, very special place in the hearts and minds of many Canadians.
Indeed, the Scottish tradition of Glengarry is still alive and well and there are still the occasional Glengarrian who can still speak Gaelic, although there are few of them left.

In Prescott County, however, which is quite different from the riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, most of my constituents are Francophones. For instance, Longueuil Township, which is located in Prescott
The Address-Mr. Boudria
County, was known as the Seigneurie de Longueuil before the Constitution Act of 1791. At the time part of New France, it is now part of the electoral district I have the honour and the privilege of representing.

The County of Russell is different again from the two others. It is near the City of Ottawa. It is the area which is perhaps the closest to me for it is near that part of the riding in which I live. I live in the Township of Cumberland in Ottawa-Carleton near Russell County. I consider myself to be a resident of that area, an area where I have spent all of my life.
I also represent a very small portion of Stormont County, namely the Island of Cornwall in which we have the Akwasasne Indian community, a people who are very, very proud but have had considerable difficulty in functioning in an area which is part of Ontario, part of Quebec and part of New York State, all within the same community.
This difficulty has been with us for some time and successive Governments have failed, in my view, to assist the residents of Akwasasne properly. It is my hope that during the next few years, together, we in this Parliament can work constructively to assist the people of Akwasasne. If we succeed, perhaps some day the people of Akwasasne will exercise their right to the franchise. No one in Akwesasne voted in the last election, period. No one voted in the previous election or ever before that. There is one instance where one person voted in Akwesasne in the 1950s, and he was chased away from the community for having done so. That is a sad reflection on our inability to help those people. If we in this Parliament could ever convince them to do otherwise, then it would be a great day. If we could convince them to vote, it means that we will have earned that respect from that which we have failed to do thus far.
Mr. Speaker, the main themes of the Throne Speech are as follows: The Prime Minister favours (1) a strong economy; (2) protection of the environment; (3) he wants Canada to continue to be a caring nation; and (4) he wants to promote the values of Canadian citizenship. Those were the four main themes, Mr. Speaker. I would like to address them one by one and give you my impressions on these themes, not as isolated concepts but in terms of the Conservative Government's past record and any action we will see in the future.

April 7, 1989
The Address-Mr. Boudria

This Government, during the last election campaign, accused the opposition Parties of making commitments which they said were not in the best interests of Canada. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) chastised the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and told him he was making promises he should not be making. Some very astute people in the media said to the Prime Minister: "Haven't you made promises?" "Oh, no," said the Prime Minister, "that is not the same. When I make promises, they are not really promises. They are commitments. We already have all that money in the Budget. We already have all that money in the Estimates, and of course we will deliver on everything we have committed to".
There are rumblings across the way that not only will they not be delivering on those promises, but they will cut back on what Canadians have already. For instance, the constituency I represent and the one represented by my distinguished colleague, the Hon. Member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Kilger), are served by VIA Rail. It is very important for our area. We are now hearing that there will be severe cut-backs, if not a total shut-down of that Crown corporation, at a time when the service is being more and more utilized by the Canadian public. There has been an increase in use in the last 12 months at VIA Rail of in excess of 10 per cent. If we did not have a VIA Rail, we would probably be planning to build one right now. Of course we would want it better than the way it is working. That is true of most things, but that does not mean that we should be shutting it down at the time that we are now.
Let us look at what the Government was promising to Canadians in the period between May 30 and September 30, 1988-1 am sorry, I should retract that, the commitments that the Conservative Government of Canada was making, because we have been told by the Prime Minister, and we would never want to contradict him, that they are not promises but commitments.
On May 30 in Ottawa, the Minister responsible for multiculturalism promised $62 million of funding for multiculturalism over five years. I am waiting to see whether that will stay in the Budget.
On May 31 in Calgary, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) promised $12 million for the emergency drought relief program for prairie farmers. We all know how poorly that program is being administered.
On June 3, 1988, in Montreal the Prime Minister promised $110 million for clean up of the St. Lawrence.
On June 7 in Ottawa, the Minister of National Health and Welfare promised $40 million for victims of family violence.
On June 7, the Secretary of State at that time, the Hon. Member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Bouchard), promised $1.4 billion federal funding for teaching and promotion of bilingualism. That is a bit much coming from that gentleman.
On June 8 in Winnipeg, the Minister of Health promised $129 million for an AIDS research program.
On June 9, the Prime Minister promised $515 million for economic development over five years in the Province of Quebec.
On June 14 in Alma, the Prime Minister-need I remind you what was happening around June 14 in the Alma/Lac-Saint-Jean area. A certain person flew across the ocean and descended upon Lac-Saint-Jean to come and give his presents to the area.

Mr. Speaker, in the Throne Speech the federal Government said we must protect the environment. Saying so is easy. It's like saying we should like apple pie. Of course we do, and of course we should or at least most people will want to protect the environment. However, when we see that during the last Parliament, during the last four years, the Government cut back staff at the Department of the Environment and either made budget cuts or at any rate refused to increase the budget and votes for the Department of the Environment in proportion to the rate of inflation, how can we be expected to take the Conservative Government seriously? Mr. Speaker, not long ago I heard on the media that an organization in the United States was going to present a medal or some kind of award to the Prime Minister for what he has done for the environment. It is nice to see that some Conservative Members are applauding, since the same group that wants to congratulate the Prime Minister has some of the biggest polluters in North

Perhaps the Tory Member who just applauded would like that kind of association, but I wouldn't, Mr. Speaker. Not me.

The Prime Minister said in the Throne Speech in his thirteenth theme that we should be a generous society. It is hard to believe that the Prime Minister is serious about this issue of being a generous society. I know that not everyone will agree with me on the following topic, but in my opinion any society who fails after this length of time to have any kind of legislation to protect those least able to help themselves-I am speaking here of the unborn-can hardly call itself a generous society under anyone's definition.
I respectfully submit that the failure of the Government to commit itself to a law on abortion-and I know we do not all agree on what the law should contain but it even failed to state that it wanted to have a law-in my view is totally inappropriate.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister told us he wanted to promote the values of Canadian citizenship. How can we take this statement seriously, when during the last three months, the Government has been using Governor General's warrants instead of facing the House? How can we, when the Prime Minister himself repudiated the Constitution of our country in this very House yesterday? I ask Hon. Members opposite: How can we take these comments seriously?

In conclusion, I want to state that in eastern Ontario, outside the general area of the City of Ottawa proper, there still is considerable hardship and considerable unemployment. This Government has promised in the Throne Speech to have regional development programs for the Atlantic, for western Canada and for northern Ontario. All previous Governments had recognized that northern and eastern Ontario needed development. This particular Government has neglected the words "eastern Ontario". We, as Liberals, have 12 out of 14 seats in eastern Ontario. We refuse to subscribe to the doctrine
dictated to us by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). We want to stand up and we want our share for this part of our great country.

This leads me into another area near and dear to the hearts of westerners, particularly those in the Province of British Columbia, that of patronage contracts and the letting of procurements. In British Columbia, from 1984 through to 1988, procurement dropped from approximately 6 per cent to approximately 4 per cent, with British Columbians having approximately 11.5 per cent of the Canadian population. Given this inequitable situation, what is the position of the Hon. Member's Party with to the letting of government contracts? Will he encourage his Party and his Leader as a Member from British Columbia to encourage equity in the area of patronage contracts and in the area of letting government procurement contracts?

Mr. Speaker, I want to apologize to the Hon. Member for having missed the first few moments of his question. Our Deputy Whip informed me of the present unfortunate situation going on outside the Chamber, and I will leave that for the present moment. I do apologize. It was not that I did not want to pay attention to his question which is undoubtedly very important.
In the area of the awarding of contracts during the last Parliament and so far in this Parliament, I have been the Government's operations critic for our Party. One of the tasks for such a role in the last Parliament was to establish constructive criticism in awards of contracts, public sector ethics, lobbying legislation and so on, as policies for our Party.

Those were announced during the last Parliament. I was one of the people who contributed to the present lobbying legislation that we now have, which has not been promulgated yet, I do not think. At least it is not in effect at the present time, but we did adopt it as a Parliament during the last Parliament. I think it was a good effort in all-Party co-operation.
In terms of other public works and supply and service contracts, some measures have been improved over the last two or three years.
I think everyone will say-and even the Prime Minister acknowledged that particularly in the beginning of his mandate in 1984-85 or so-that there were considerable difficulties in the administration of that. I am not going to get into the activities that went on, the charges and so on that have occurred. Those are there on the public record.
I think what we have to do, and some of these things have taken place already, is to ensure that we lower the threshold which is utilized in order to determine what contract goes out for public tender. We need to enforce the regulations in so far as determining what the exceptions are to those tendering procedures. There are always emergencies when we have to call a plumber in the middle of the night to repair a facility, a boiler or a heating system. I think we all recognize that this kind of situation must continue. .
We must tighten up the rules as much as we can. We must also strengthen the conflict of laws that we have not only for Members of Parliament and cabinet Minister but for some of the senior civil servants as well. I think the stricter those rules the better they will be. Some people have said that stricter conflict of interest rules will discourage people from entering public office. 1 hold exactly the opposite view. In fact, hopefully the stricter the rules, the better the system will be. If the system is better, people will be more attracted to run for public office because it will enjoy a higher level of reputation than it does at certain unfortunate times right now.

First, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to say a few words in this hour of debate that is coming to an end today on the Throne Speech. Also, I would like in the first place to take this opportunity to thank my constituents in Saint-Maurice for trusting me on November 21, 1988, when they elected me as their first Progressive Conservative MP in 97 years.
The Address-Mr. Pronovost
During the Throne Speech, Mr. Speaker, numerous references were made to all areas involving the environment, and my constituency has been very much in the headlines these last few days with the PCB spill from the Belgo plant in Shawinigan. People in my constituency have been very concerned, because this is the second toxic spill from that plant in three months and they have every reason to be disturbed. The Belgo plant in Shawinigan has been in breach of the environment laws on many occasions over these last few years, a fact that has surfaced a number of times.
You know, Mr. Speaker, I was very amazed during these last weeks to see how much the whole issue of the environment is an important one to people in my constituency and to Canadians from sea to sea.
I had the opportunity, pleasure and privilege to rise three times in this House in two days on the matter of the Saint-Maurice river pollution. I did some research to find out about the behaviour of the two Liberal Members who were my predecessors during the last 25 years.
To my great stupefaction, Mr. Speaker, and to the shame of my constituents, we have found that in 25 years of Liberal government, not once did these two Liberal Members, Mr. Chretien and Mr. Grondin, find a way to rise in this House to condemn the pollution and very deteriorated state of the Saint-Maurice river.
It was my pleasure to do so on three occasions in two days. And the constituents in Saint-Maurice wondered why Jean Chretien did not do that. Why did he not rise in this House during the 20 years he represented us here, why he did not do so? We understood why last year, Mr. Speaker, when Jean Chretien was elected to the board of Consolidated Bathurst. We are paying the price for 21 years of silence. Jean Chretien was rewarded for not saying a word in this House and for having let the Saint-Maurice river become one of the most polluted in Canada. Today, Mr. Speaker, pollutants are often spilled in the Saint-Maurice river. Consolidated Bathurst, Belgo Division, has never had any trouble with the federal government.
We now have a new Minister of the Environment (M. Lucien Bouchard), who will not be pushed around. The new Minister of the Environment is not afraid of Consolidated Bathurst. He has said in this House that if Consolidated Bathurst has broken the law, the Federal government will take legal proceedings. During 25 years of silence, never did Jean Chretien, who was Minister of Finance, who headed about every Department, never did Jean Chretien, with all his power and influence, dare say such a thing. The citizens of Saint-Maurice sure fixed his wagon along with that of his gang on November 21

last when the Liberal candidate finished third, behind the socialist candidate.
In a by-election held in my riding barely two years ago, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal candidate got 65 percent of the vote. In two years, the Liberal Party in my riding, a so-called Liberal stronghold has fallen to 19 percent. And the next time, Mr. Speaker, he will lose his deposit!
The environment was a major issue during the election campaign. It was therefore conforting to see the Leader of the Opposition (M. Turner), contrary to the New Democrats for whom Quebec does not exist as far as pollution is concerned and who remained silent, rise in this House and, although he was a bit mixed up, pronounced for the first time in his life the name of the city of Shawinigan. He has been haunted by the city of
Shawiningan for the past four years! He nevertheless rose to ask a question about pollution in the Saint-Mau-rice River. However, the Leader of the Opposition does not know, Mr. Speaker, that the Saint-Maurice river is under provincial jurisdiction, that Consolidated Bathurst is a provincially chartered corporation. But the fact remains that, although this matter comes under provincial jurisdiction, the Minister of the Environment has looked into the problem, into the whole issue.
